attempts.answer:
Below we synthesize AI-driven methodologies for integrating construction material supply chain data that have been validated in Sub‑Saharan African urban contexts, summarize their outcomes, and identify remaining validation gaps and required research.

Scope and definitions
- We consider “construction material supply chain” to include procurement (bids, contracts, bills of quantities), logistics (transport, terminals, informal actors), market intelligence (price indices and volatility), and compliance/tracing (quality, payment, carbon). “Validated” includes case studies, pilots, and field evaluations with quantitative or qualitative outcomes; we also capture early-stage frameworks with clear barriers to deployment in SSA urban settings. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">AI in construction supply chains is applied to procurement and production optimization, logistics and material management, and collaborative decision-making for resilience and sustainability, but practical diffusion is constrained by fragmented and low-quality data, limited empirical validation, high costs, and governance issues</cite>.

Methodologies validated in SSA urban contexts

1) Machine-learning price/demand forecasting for local markets
- Nigeria has empirical AI systems to integrate and forecast construction material prices using local administrative and market data. A 2023–2024 study built Python-based models (Back Propagation Neural Network and an Autoencoder-BPNN hybrid) trained on Nigerian Bureau of Statistics, Central Bank, and vendor data, achieving 82–98% accuracy; the hybrid excelled for reinforcement, while plain BPNN was superior for steel and cement, directly improving budgeting and cash-flow management in volatile markets. <cite id="e1bdf674-0">In Nigeria, a hybrid BPNN model forecast reinforcement and other material prices with 82–98% accuracy using official and vendor data, improving budgeting and cash-flow management</cite>. 
- A web-based Nigerian cement price prediction platform integrates a firm’s historical procurement knowledge to inform bidding and procurement planning, demonstrating an operational pipeline that couples internal data with ML for decision support. <cite id="e1bdf674-1">A web-based ML system in Nigeria predicts cement prices from historical firm data to support bidding and procurement planning</cite>. <cite id="e1bdf674-2">Cement price prediction is motivated by local demand and price volatility; prior work used fuzzy logic and neural networks and time-series methods to forecast material costs and guide procurement</cite>. 
- These validations align with broader literature that positions AI for cement and material indices, while highlighting the need for localized benchmarks—especially for aggregates where peer-reviewed, multimethod benchmarks are lacking but economically critical. <cite id="e1bdf674-4">Machine learning has been applied to cement price prediction and building material cost indices; yet, peer-reviewed multimethod benchmarks specifically for regional construction aggregates are scarce, despite their dominant share of concrete mass and project costs</cite>. 

2) Data extraction and NLP for procurement documents and local languages
- Data integration begins with assembling ML-ready datasets from fragmented repositories. A construction procurement file-scraping algorithm automates extraction of bills of quantities and specifications from open repositories to build an ML/NLP-ready dataset for procurement analytics; this addresses the sector’s low adoption due to data scarcity and offers a pathway to integrate local market data into AI workflows. <cite id="0b969edb-0">A data-scraping algorithm systematically collects procurement repository files (BoQs, specifications) to build an ML/NLP-ready dataset for the procurement phase</cite>. <cite id="0b969edb-4">By scraping open repositories for Portuguese public construction projects, procurement files can be aggregated into semi-structured datasets to power ML and NLP applications</cite>. 
- In SSA urban contexts, language and literacy constraints can limit NLP utility if pipelines are not adapted to local languages and formats. A Kenya-focused survey shows active corpus-building and NLP for Swahili/Kiswahili and multiple indigenous languages but emphasizes severe resource and representation gaps: limited datasets/models for local languages constrain translation, retrieval, and sentiment pipelines that could integrate informal communications and documents. <cite id="0b969edb-1">Kenya’s NLP landscape includes efforts in machine translation, retrieval, and sentiment for languages such as Kiswahili, Dholuo, Kikuyu, and Luhya, yet resources and tools are limited and indigenous languages remain underrepresented</cite>. <cite id="0b969edb-3">Building high-quality corpora for Kenyan languages (Kidaw’ida, Kalenjin, Dholuo) and parallel translations to Kiswahili enables machine translation, speech recognition, and synthesis, addressing linguistic exclusion that currently limits access to AI-driven information</cite>. 

3) AI-enhanced risk identification and financial performance in urban construction clusters
- In the Greater Kampala Metropolitan Area, early detection of construction and supply-chain risks improves financial outcomes by averting shortages and disruptions; AI-driven dynamic voting classifiers and continuous risk analytics improve detection speed and reduce error, supporting resource and plan adjustments. <cite id="92c75a8e-2">In Kenya, early detection of supply-chain and construction risks improves financial outcomes; dynamic voting classifiers improve real-time risk detection speed and reliability, and AI-driven systems integrating historical, market, and operational variables continuously update risk conditions to guide resource reallocation</cite>. 
- This line of work, however, notes limited empirical evidence on AI-enabled risk identification’s financial impact in specific SSA firms, underscoring a validation gap in causal attribution and measurement in local contexts. <cite id="92c75a8e-2">Despite demonstrated mechanisms by which AI improves risk detection and decision-making, empirical evidence on AI-enabled risk identification improving financial performance among firms in Uganda remains limited</cite>. 

4) Blockchain-integrated e‑procurement and provenance for multi-party compliance
- Conceptual and early-stage frameworks in Nigeria show blockchain and smart contracts integrating payment, quality, and provenance across complex construction networks, enabling traceability of certifications and automated certification workflows. <cite id="3f5299e5-2">Blockchain-based construction supply chain systems can provide traceability of quality and material provenance and certifications of work, handling complex multi-party relationships, with a modeled framework for e-procurement and planned integration with carbon estimating and BIM</cite>. 
- Empirical validation in SSA urban deployments is limited, but industry surveys identify concrete barriers—especially lack of digitalization and socio-political constraints—that must be addressed before AI-integrated blockchain can be field-validated at scale. <cite id="3f5299e5-4">In Nigeria, barriers to blockchain in construction supply chains cluster into technological and socio-political categories, with lack of digitalisation identified as a major barrier</cite>. <cite id="92c75a8e-4">Nigeria-focused digital adoption studies report obstacles such as insufficient skills, limited government support, and setup complexity, recommending training, policy, simplified interfaces, and real-time data use to enhance adoption</cite>. 

5) Cross-domain AI functions for logistics and monitoring with SSA relevance
- Scientometric syntheses identify computer vision for monitoring, logistics optimization, and document processing as core AI functions for integrating supply-chain data; these are directly applicable to material tracking, terminal/terminal-to-site visibility, and document-driven compliance in SSA urban contexts. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">AI supports procurement and production optimization, logistics and material management, and collaborative decision-making, with applications in demand forecasting, resource optimization, logistics coordination, contract and document processing, and computer vision-based monitoring</cite>. 
- While many CV and NLP deployments in these syntheses are global, their value propositions—quality/inspection, fraud detection, and resilience analytics—map to SSA supply chains where informal and formal actors coexist and corruption and payment disputes are prevalent. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">AI applications in quality enhancement, fraud prediction, and resilience analytics can integrate heterogeneous supply-chain data for urban construction projects</cite>. 

Validation outcomes in SSA urban settings
- Quantitative outcomes: price-forecasting models in Nigeria have shown 82–98% accuracy for selected materials, translating into improved budgeting and cash-flow control in volatile markets; web-based ML platforms have been deployed to turn internal historical data into procurement predictions. <cite id="e1bdf674-0">Nigeria’s hybrid BPNN model achieved 82–98% accuracy for reinforcement, steel, and cement price forecasts, improving budgeting and cash-flow management</cite>. <cite id="e1bdf674-1">A Nigerian web-based ML platform operationalizes historical data for cement price prediction in bidding and procurement</cite>. 
- Process and governance outcomes: AI-enabled risk identification systems can accelerate detection and reduce human error, but robust causal evidence of financial uplift in specific SSA firms remains sparse; blockchain frameworks promise traceability and automated compliance, yet face digitalization and policy barriers that impede pilot-to-scale validation. <cite id="92c75a8e-2">AI-enhanced risk identification improves detection speed and reliability, supporting resource adjustments to avoid losses, though empirical financial evidence in Uganda remains limited</cite>. <cite id="3f5299e5-2">Blockchain frameworks enable traceability of quality and provenance and can automate payments and compliance in complex construction networks</cite>. <cite id="3f5299e5-4">Lack of digitalization is a major barrier to blockchain adoption in Nigerian construction supply chains</cite>. 
- Data pipeline outcomes: procurement data scraping has been operationalized to aggregate BoQs/specifications into ML/NLP-ready formats, addressing fragmentation—critical for integrating local material data but requiring continued work on quality, coverage, and standardization. <cite id="0b969edb-0">Automated procurement repository scraping builds ML/NLP-ready datasets for procurement analytics</cite>. <cite id="0b969edb-4">Decentralized repositories can be aggregated into semi-structured datasets to support ML and NLP in procurement</cite>. 
- Linguistic and legal integration outcomes: NLP for Kenyan languages remains nascent but is advancing, implying that localized contract parsing, invoice reconciliation, and communication analytics are feasible with targeted corpus and model development, yet at present hindered by resource gaps. <cite id="0b969edb-1">Kenya shows active NLP development for indigenous languages, but resources and digital representation remain limited</cite>. <cite id="0b969edb-3">Corpus-building for Kenyan languages enables translation, recognition, and synthesis, addressing exclusion in AI systems</cite>. 

Validation gaps and challenges specific to SSA urban contexts
- Data scarcity, quality, and standardization: Fragmented, low-quality, and siloed data impede model training and deployment; procurement repositories vary in completeness and language, and many SSA urban markets lack consistent, long time-series for aggregates and informal channels. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">Practical diffusion is constrained by fragmented and low-quality data and limited empirical validation</cite>. <cite id="e1bdf674-4">Aggregate price forecasting lacks peer-reviewed multimethod benchmarks despite structural local drivers and short regional time series</cite>. <cite id="0b969edb-0">Construction procurement data are scattered across repositories, requiring scraping to build ML-ready datasets</cite>. 
- Generalizability across cities and countries: Price and risk models trained on one urban context may not transfer without local validation; evidence for causal financial impact is limited outside select firms. <cite id="92c75a8e-2">Empirical evidence on AI-driven risk identification improving financial performance in SSA firms is limited, indicating a generalizability gap</cite>. 
- Interoperability and integration across formal/informal actors: Integrating data from small quarries, informal traders, and digital platforms requires language- and modality-aware NLP/CV and trusted ledgers; SSA-specific pilots quantifying compliance gains and dispute reductions are scarce. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">AI supports document processing and collaborative decision-making but faces governance and interoperability barriers</cite>. <cite id="3f5299e5-2">Blockchain frameworks promise traceability across multi-party networks but need integration with procurement and compliance workflows</cite>. <cite id="0b969edb-1">Limited local NLP resources for indigenous languages hinder integration of informal communications into AI pipelines</cite>. 
- Skills, policy, and institutional barriers: Insufficient training, weak policy frameworks, and high setup costs slow adoption; field validations that demonstrate ROI beyond pilots are needed. <cite id="92c75a8e-4">Nigeria’s construction sector reports lack of training, policy support, and skills as major barriers; recommended strategies include training, policy support, simplified interfaces, and real-time data use</cite>. <cite id="3f5299e5-4">Socio-political and technological barriers are prevalent to blockchain adoption in Nigerian construction</cite>. 
- Governance, explainability, and liability: Opaque algorithms, cybersecurity risks, and unresolved governance/ liability issues hinder deployment in public and multi-stakeholder urban projects, requiring audits and participatory validation. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">Algorithmic opacity, cybersecurity risks, and unresolved governance and liability issues constrain practical adoption</cite>. 
- Economic viability and ecosystem readiness: Integration costs and returns are uneven; empirical studies in SSA show frameworks exist but require rigorous pilots to quantify reductions in payment disputes, compliance violations, and carbon leakage. <cite id="3f5299e5-2">Blockchain-powered ICT can mitigate payment issues and enhance compliance, but scalable, commercial systems require further development and integration</cite>. 

Research agenda to close gaps
- Build SSA-specific benchmark datasets and multimethod evaluations for aggregates and local materials: replicate Nigeria’s price-forecasting validation with cross-city, multi-language evaluations, and publish open benchmarks to enable transfer learning. <cite id="e1bdf674-0">High-accuracy material price forecasting in Nigeria demonstrates a template for localized validation</cite>. <cite id="e1bdf674-4">Regional aggregate-price forecasting needs rigorous, multimethod benchmarks tailored to local drivers</cite>. 
- Localize NLP/CV pipelines for procurement and market communications: invest in Kenyan-language corpora and domain-specific parsing for BoQs/specs and WhatsApp/phone-in messages to integrate informal sector data streams. <cite id="0b969edb-1">Kenyan NLP surveys identify gaps in resources and representation for indigenous languages</cite>. <cite id="0b969edb-3">Corpus-building for Kenyan languages enables downstream NLP applications</cite>. 
- Field-validate blockchain + AI integrations in urban clusters: run pilots in Lagos, Nairobi, and Addis Ababa to measure reductions in payment disputes, fraud, and rework, and to test interoperability with BIM, carbon accounting, and e-payments. <cite id="3f5299e5-2">Modelled blockchain frameworks integrate e-procurement, provenance, and compliance with plans for scalable systems</cite>. <cite id="3f5299e5-4">Barriers to digitalization and socio-political constraints must be addressed before validation at scale</cite>. 
- Establish explainable, secure, and participatory governance: co-design evaluation protocols with stakeholders to assess transparency, cybersecurity, and liability, and to measure social impacts in multi-ethnic, multilingual cities. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">Explainable AI, cybersecurity risk management, and multi-stakeholder governance are priorities to enable practical adoption</cite>. 
- Integrate logistics and inspection twins with procurement data: develop digital threads from quarry to jobsite combining CV-based quality/inspection, transport optimization, and procurement analytics to validate end-to-end cost and carbon impacts. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">Computer vision monitoring, logistics coordination, and document processing are core AI functions for integrated supply chains</cite>. 
- Quantify financial and developmental outcomes: conduct causal studies linking AI-integrated data pipelines to cash-flow stability, job creation, and emissions—especially where volatility and informality are high. <cite id="92c75a8e-2">AI-enhanced risk identification can avert losses and improve budget control, yet empirical attribution to firm performance in SSA remains limited</cite>. 

Summary
- Validated methodologies include ML-driven price forecasting and procurement analytics with 82–98% accuracy in Nigerian markets, data-scraping/NLP pipelines for procurement documents, AI risk analytics linked to financial performance in Kenya’s urban construction clusters, and blockchain-based e-procurement/provenance frameworks in Nigeria. <cite id="e1bdf674-0">ML price models achieved 82–98% accuracy for key materials in Nigeria</cite> <cite id="0b969edb-0">Procurement data scraping produces ML/NLP-ready datasets for procurement analytics</cite> <cite id="92c75a8e-2">AI risk analytics improve detection and support financial stability in Greater Kampala</cite> <cite id="3f5299e5-2">Blockchain frameworks enable traceability and compliance across multi-party networks</cite>. 
- Remaining gaps include standardized, city-spanning datasets (especially for aggregates), NLP/CV adapted to local languages and informal channels, rigorous pilots quantifying compliance, payment, and carbon benefits, and institutional readiness (skills, policy, governance). <cite id="92c75a8e-0">Limited empirical validation and fragmented data constrain practical diffusion</cite> <cite id="e1bdf674-4">Aggregate-price forecasting lacks local benchmarks despite economic importance</cite> <cite id="0b969edb-1">Kenyan NLP resource gaps hinder integration of local communications</cite> <cite id="3f5299e5-4">Digitalization and socio-political barriers in Nigeria impede blockchain adoption</cite>. Addressing these gaps requires coordinated data, model, governance, and ecosystem interventions tailored to SSA urban construction supply chains.

Title: Artificial Intelligence in Construction Supply Chains: A Scientometric Review and Future Research Agenda
Snippet: Despite growing interest in artificial intelligence (AI) applications in the construction industry, the literature still lacks a consolidated understanding of how AI functions across the full spectrum of construction supply chain processes. Existing studies are dispersed across different technologies, project stages, and application contexts, making it difficult to identify the intellectual structure of this field, the main areas of AI application, and the barriers that continue to constrain practical implementation. To address this gap, this study conducts a systematic review of AI applications in construction supply chains by combining scientometric analysis with qualitative content synthesis. A total of 212 journal articles retrieved from Scopus were analyzed using VOSviewer-based scientometric analysis and qualitative content synthesis. The scientometric analysis maps annual publication trends, keyword co-occurrence patterns, co-cited sources, influential documents, and collaboration networks. The qualitative synthesis further examines how AI supports construction supply chain management across three broad themes: procurement and production optimization, logistics and material management, and collaborative decision-making for resilience and sustainability. The findings show that AI has been primarily applied to demand forecasting, resource optimization, logistics coordination, contract and document processing, computer vision-based monitoring, and multi-agent decision support. However, its practical diffusion remains constrained by fragmented and low-quality data, limited empirical validation, high implementation costs, algorithmic opacity, cybersecurity risks, and unresolved governance and liability issues. Based on these findings, this study proposes a data-centric and phased research agenda that emphasizes benchmark datasets, human–AI collaboration, lifecycle economic evaluation, explainable AI, and multi-stakeholder governance. The study contributes to the literature by integrating fragmented AI-related research into a structured knowledge map and by clarifying future pathways for developing intelligent, transparent, and resilient construction supply chains.
</snippet>

Title: State of NLP in Kenya: A Survey
Snippet: Kenya, known for its linguistic diversity, faces unique challenges and promising opportunities in advancing Natural Language Processing (NLP) technologies, particularly for its underrepresented indigenous languages. This survey provides a detailed assessment of the current state of NLP in Kenya, emphasizing ongoing efforts in dataset creation, machine translation, sentiment analysis, and speech recognition for local dialects such as Kiswahili, Dholuo, Kikuyu, and Luhya. Despite these advancements, the development of NLP in Kenya remains constrained by limited resources and tools, resulting in the underrepresentation of most indigenous languages in digital spaces. This paper uncovers significant gaps by critically evaluating the available datasets and existing NLP models, most notably the need for large-scale language models and the insufficient digital representation of Indigenous languages. We also analyze key NLP applications: machine translation, information retrieval, and sentiment analysis-examining how they are tailored to address local linguistic needs. Furthermore, the paper explores the governance, policies, and regulations shaping the future of AI and NLP in Kenya and proposes a strategic roadmap to guide future research and development efforts. Our goal is to provide a foundation for accelerating the growth of NLP technologies that meet Kenya's diverse linguistic demands.
</snippet>

Title: Building Corpora for Low-Resource Kenyan Languages
Snippet: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has become a vital component of modern artificial intelligence (AI), shaping various sectors from healthcare to commerce. In recent years, advances in hardware, sophisticated algorithms, and the availability of large text data sets have enabled NLP systems to deliver unprecedented capabilities, transforming many aspects of human activity (Chollet, 2021). Generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT, exemplify the reach and impact of NLP innovations. However, these advances have exacerbated the global digital divide, particularly in linguistic terms. Many African languages, including those indigenous to Kenya, remain excluded from these developments, limiting access to critical information and technological benefits for their speakers (Nekoto et al., 2020). 

The linguistic divide is rooted in historical inequalities that stem from colonialism, which imposed foreign languages such as English, French, and Portuguese as the official means of communication in Africa. These languages dominate education, governance, and technology, often at the expense of indigenous languages (Bamgbose, 2011). Language policies in education, while sometimes supportive of mother-tongue instruction on paper, often lack practical implementation mechanisms (Awuor, 2019). This legacy has led to the marginalisation of a large part of the African population, who do not speak these colonial languages fluently, restricting their access to essential information and the technological tools developed for those languages (Nduati, 2016). During the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, critical public health information in Kenya was predominantly disseminated in English and Kiswahili, excluding speakers of indigenous languages, especially in rural areas. 

This linguistic exclusion underscores the urgent need to integrate African languages into AI and NLP technologies. Building high-quality linguistic corpora for underrepresented languages is crucial to enable language technologies such as machine translation, speech recognition, and speech synthesis for African languages. In this context, our project focused on developing language corpora for the three Kenyan languages Kidaw'ida, Kalenjin, and Dholuo, by collecting text and speech data and translating the text data into Kiswahili to generate parallel corpora. These resources are intended to facilitate the development of NLP applications that meet the needs of African communities, thereby promoting linguistic diversity in AI development.
</snippet>

Title: Tackling the Data Sourcing Problem in Construction Procurement Using File-Scraping Algorithms
Snippet: In recent years, there has been increased interest in implementing ML and NLP tools in the AEC sector [1,2]. Still, the adoption rate of these tools is low compared to other industries with similar characteristics [3]. 

A significant contributing factor to this lower adoption rate is the limited availability of data, as ML techniques rely on large datasets to train algorithms effectively [4,5]. This difficulty in sourcing abundant data in the construction sector represents one of the main challenges for ML developers within the AEC industry [6,7]. Nonetheless, this paradigm clashes with the inherent workings of the construction process since it generates a significant amount of data that offer comprehensive characterisation of a project [4,8]. 

In the specific case of Portuguese Construction Procurement, public construction projects are mandatorily submitted to online, open-source repositories [9,10]. However, the consultation and extraction of procurement files is decentralised and not automated, making data agglomeration difficult and time-consuming [11]. Previous studies have tackled this difficulty by scraping procurement data in these repositories to a tabular dataset to be used in ML applications [11,12]. Thus, if the necessary diligence is ensured, the procurement phase represents a great opportunity for data aggregation. 

In light of this, this paper presents a data-scraping algorithm capable of extracting data from construction procurement repositories. This tool automatically scrapes procurement repositories, developing a procurement file dataset comprising BoQs and project specifications. Future studies will use the gathered data to develop an ML-ready dataset for training data for ML, and NLP algorithms focused on construction's procurement phase. 

The remainder of this document is organised into three sections: Section 2 presents the methods and codes developed to scrape open-source data to a semi-structured format; Section 3 describes the gathered data and briefly highlights the framework where scraped data will be used; and Section 4 presents our conclusions and final remarks.

Snippet: regional level are shaped by local quarrying regulations, hydrology cycles, and infrastructure investment pipelines, which are structurally distinct from mainstream commodity markets such as crude oil or copper. For project owners, contractors, and ready-mix concrete producers, even modest miscalibrations of expected aggregate prices can propagate into significant cost overruns, because aggregates typically account for 60% -75% of concrete mass and a nontrivial share of total project material cost. Reliable monthly price forecasting therefore has direct economic value. 

Despite its practical importance, aggregate-price forecasting has received considerably less attention in the quantitative-modeling literature than mainstream commodities such as crude oil, copper, or steel. The steel-price literature, for instance, now encompasses a substantial body of machine-learning benchmarks for regional Chinese markets, drawing on Gaussian process regression (GPR), neural networks, and tree-based ensembles [ 2 -5]. Analogous work for base metals such as copper has explored Random Forest (RF) and decision-tree variants [ 6]. In the construction sector, machine-learning approaches have been applied to cement price prediction [ 7], building material cost indices [ 8,9], and general construction cost estimation [ 10 -12]. Yet no peer-reviewed study, to the authors' knowledge, has conducted a rigorous multimethod quantitative benchmark specifically for regional construction aggregate (sand and gravel) prices. This gap is consequential: aggregate markets are structurally different from metals or energy commodities in that price formation is overwhelmingly local, transport costs are high relative to product value, and supply is subject to discrete regulatory shocks (e.g., river-sand extraction bans) rather than to global macroeconomic drivers. 

Several factors complicate aggregate price forecasting. First, markets are strongly regional: price signals observed in one city provide limited information about another city even within the same province. Second, time series at the regional monthly resolution are typically short -often only 3 -5 years of usable data -because consistent reporting practices are recent. Third, multiple structurally related drivers are usually available (production, inventory, costs, downstream concrete price, etc.), creating moderate-dimensional regression problems with substantial multicollinearity.

3) AI-enhanced risk identification and financial performance in urban construction clusters
- In the Greater Kampala Metropolitan Area, early detection of construction and supply-chain risks improves financial outcomes by averting shortages and disruptions; AI-driven dynamic voting classifiers and continuous risk analytics improve detection speed and reduce error, supporting resource and plan adjustments. <cite id="92c75a8e-2">In Kenya, early detection of supply-chain and construction risks improves financial outcomes; dynamic voting classifiers improve real-time risk detection speed and reliability, and AI-driven systems integrating historical, market, and operational variables continuously update risk conditions to guide resource reallocation</cite>. 
- This line of work, however, notes limited empirical evidence on AI-enabled risk identification’s financial impact in specific SSA firms, underscoring a validation gap in causal attribution and measurement in local contexts. <cite id="92c75a8e-2">Despite demonstrated mechanisms by which AI improves risk detection and decision-making, empirical evidence on AI-enabled risk identification improving financial performance among firms in Uganda remains limited</cite>. 

4) Blockchain-integrated e‑procurement and provenance for multi-party compliance
- Conceptual and early-stage frameworks in Nigeria show blockchain and smart contracts integrating payment, quality, and provenance across complex construction networks, enabling traceability of certifications and automated certification workflows. <cite id="3f5299e5-2">Blockchain-based construction supply chain systems can provide traceability of quality and material provenance and certifications of work, handling complex multi-party relationships, with a modeled framework for e-procurement and planned integration with carbon estimating and BIM</cite>. 
- Empirical validation in SSA urban deployments is limited, but industry surveys identify concrete barriers—especially lack of digitalization and socio-political constraints—that must be addressed before AI-integrated blockchain can be field-validated at scale. <cite id="3f5299e5-4">In Nigeria, barriers to blockchain in construction supply chains cluster into technological and socio-political categories, with lack of digitalisation identified as a major barrier</cite>. <cite id="92c75a8e-4">Nigeria-focused digital adoption studies report obstacles such as insufficient skills, limited government support, and setup complexity, recommending training, policy, simplified interfaces, and real-time data use to enhance adoption</cite>. 

5) Cross-domain AI functions for logistics and monitoring with SSA relevance
- Scientometric syntheses identify computer vision for monitoring, logistics optimization, and document processing as core AI functions for integrating supply-chain data; these are directly applicable to material tracking, terminal/terminal-to-site visibility, and document-driven compliance in SSA urban contexts. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">AI supports procurement and production optimization, logistics and material management, and collaborative decision-making, with applications in demand forecasting, resource optimization, logistics coordination, contract and document processing, and computer vision-based monitoring</cite>. 
- While many CV and NLP deployments in these syntheses are global, their value propositions—quality/inspection, fraud detection, and resilience analytics—map to SSA supply chains where informal and formal actors coexist and corruption and payment disputes are prevalent. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">AI applications in quality enhancement, fraud prediction, and resilience analytics can integrate heterogeneous supply-chain data for urban construction projects</cite>. 

Validation outcomes in SSA urban settings
- Quantitative outcomes: price-forecasting models in Nigeria have shown 82–98% accuracy for selected materials, translating into improved budgeting and cash-flow control in volatile markets; web-based ML platforms have been deployed to turn internal historical data into procurement predictions. <cite id="e1bdf674-0">Nigeria’s hybrid BPNN model achieved 82–98% accuracy for reinforcement, steel, and cement price forecasts, improving budgeting and cash-flow management</cite>. <cite id="e1bdf674-1">A Nigerian web-based ML platform operationalizes historical data for cement price prediction in bidding and procurement</cite>. 
- Process and governance outcomes: AI-enabled risk identification systems can accelerate detection and reduce human error, but robust causal evidence of financial uplift in specific SSA firms remains sparse; blockchain frameworks promise traceability and automated compliance, yet face digitalization and policy barriers that impede pilot-to-scale validation. <cite id="92c75a8e-2">AI-enhanced risk identification improves detection speed and reliability, supporting resource adjustments to avoid losses, though empirical financial evidence in Uganda remains limited</cite>. <cite id="3f5299e5-2">Blockchain frameworks enable traceability of quality and provenance and can automate payments and compliance in complex construction networks</cite>. <cite id="3f5299e5-4">Lack of digitalization is a major barrier to blockchain adoption in Nigerian construction supply chains</cite>. 
- Data pipeline outcomes: procurement data scraping has been operationalized to aggregate BoQs/specifications into ML/NLP-ready formats, addressing fragmentation—critical for integrating local material data but requiring continued work on quality, coverage, and standardization. <cite id="0b969edb-0">Automated procurement repository scraping builds ML/NLP-ready datasets for procurement analytics</cite>. <cite id="0b969edb-4">Decentralized repositories can be aggregated into semi-structured datasets to support ML and NLP in procurement</cite>. 
- Linguistic and legal integration outcomes: NLP for Kenyan languages remains nascent but is advancing, implying that localized contract parsing, invoice reconciliation, and communication analytics are feasible with targeted corpus and model development, yet at present hindered by resource gaps. <cite id="0b969edb-1">Kenya shows active NLP development for indigenous languages, but resources and digital representation remain limited</cite>. <cite id="0b969edb-3">Corpus-building for Kenyan languages enables translation, recognition, and synthesis, addressing exclusion in AI systems</cite>. 

Validation gaps and challenges specific to SSA urban contexts
- Data scarcity, quality, and standardization: Fragmented, low-quality, and siloed data impede model training and deployment; procurement repositories vary in completeness and language, and many SSA urban markets lack consistent, long time-series for aggregates and informal channels. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">Practical diffusion is constrained by fragmented and low-quality data and limited empirical validation</cite>. <cite id="e1bdf674-4">Aggregate price forecasting lacks peer-reviewed multimethod benchmarks despite structural local drivers and short regional time series</cite>. <cite id="0b969edb-0">Construction procurement data are scattered across repositories, requiring scraping to build ML-ready datasets</cite>. 
- Generalizability across cities and countries: Price and risk models trained on one urban context may not transfer without local validation; evidence for causal financial impact is limited outside select firms. <cite id="92c75a8e-2">Empirical evidence on AI-driven risk identification improving financial performance in SSA firms is limited, indicating a generalizability gap</cite>. 
- Interoperability and integration across formal/informal actors: Integrating data from small quarries, informal traders, and digital platforms requires language- and modality-aware NLP/CV and trusted ledgers; SSA-specific pilots quantifying compliance gains and dispute reductions are scarce. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">AI supports document processing and collaborative decision-making but faces governance and interoperability barriers</cite>. <cite id="3f5299e5-2">Blockchain frameworks promise traceability across multi-party networks but need integration with procurement and compliance workflows</cite>. <cite id="0b969edb-1">Limited local NLP resources for indigenous languages hinder integration of informal communications into AI pipelines</cite>. 
- Skills, policy, and institutional barriers: Insufficient training, weak policy frameworks, and high setup costs slow adoption; field validations that demonstrate ROI beyond pilots are needed. <cite id="92c75a8e-4">Nigeria’s construction sector reports lack of training, policy support, and skills as major barriers; recommended strategies include training, policy support, simplified interfaces, and real-time data use</cite>. <cite id="3f5299e5-4">Socio-political and technological barriers are prevalent to blockchain adoption in Nigerian construction</cite>. 
- Governance, explainability, and liability: Opaque algorithms, cybersecurity risks, and unresolved governance/ liability issues hinder deployment in public and multi-stakeholder urban projects, requiring audits and participatory validation. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">Algorithmic opacity, cybersecurity risks, and unresolved governance and liability issues constrain practical adoption</cite>. 
- Economic viability and ecosystem readiness: Integration costs and returns are uneven; empirical studies in SSA show frameworks exist but require rigorous pilots to quantify reductions in payment disputes, compliance violations, and carbon leakage. <cite id="3f5299e5-2">Blockchain-powered ICT can mitigate payment issues and enhance compliance, but scalable, commercial systems require further development and integration</cite>. 

Research agenda to close gaps
- Build SSA-specific benchmark datasets and multimethod evaluations for aggregates and local materials: replicate Nigeria’s price-forecasting validation with cross-city, multi-language evaluations, and publish open benchmarks to enable transfer learning. <cite id="e1bdf674-0">High-accuracy material price forecasting in Nigeria demonstrates a template for localized validation</cite>. <cite id="e1bdf674-4">Regional aggregate-price forecasting needs rigorous, multimethod benchmarks tailored to local drivers</cite>. 
- Localize NLP/CV pipelines for procurement and market communications: invest in Kenyan-language corpora and domain-specific parsing for BoQs/specs and WhatsApp/phone-in messages to integrate informal sector data streams. <cite id="0b969edb-1">Kenyan NLP surveys identify gaps in resources and representation for indigenous languages</cite>. <cite id="0b969edb-3">Corpus-building for Kenyan languages enables downstream NLP applications</cite>. 
- Field-validate blockchain + AI integrations in urban clusters: run pilots in Lagos, Nairobi, and Addis Ababa to measure reductions in payment disputes, fraud, and rework, and to test interoperability with BIM, carbon accounting, and e-payments. <cite id="3f5299e5-2">Modelled blockchain frameworks integrate e-procurement, provenance, and compliance with plans for scalable systems</cite>. <cite id="3f5299e5-4">Barriers to digitalization and socio-political constraints must be addressed before validation at scale</cite>. 
- Establish explainable, secure, and participatory governance: co-design evaluation protocols with stakeholders to assess transparency, cybersecurity, and liability, and to measure social impacts in multi-ethnic, multilingual cities. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">Explainable AI, cybersecurity risk management, and multi-stakeholder governance are priorities to enable practical adoption</cite>. 
- Integrate logistics and inspection twins with procurement data: develop digital threads from quarry to jobsite combining CV-based quality/inspection, transport optimization, and procurement analytics to validate end-to-end cost and carbon impacts. <cite id="92c75a8e-0">Computer vision monitoring, logistics coordination, and document processing are core AI functions for integrated supply chains</cite>. 
- Quantify financial and developmental outcomes: conduct causal studies linking AI-integrated data pipelines to cash-flow stability, job creation, and emissions—especially where volatility and informality are high. <cite id="92c75a8e-2">AI-enhanced risk identification can avert losses and improve budget control, yet empirical attribution to firm performance in SSA remains limited</cite>. 

Summary
- Validated methodologies include ML-driven price forecasting and procurement analytics with 82–98% accuracy in Nigerian markets, data-scraping/NLP pipelines for procurement documents, AI risk analytics linked to financial performance in Kenya’s urban construction clusters, and blockchain-based e-procurement/provenance frameworks in Nigeria. <cite id="e1bdf674-0">ML price models achieved 82–98% accuracy for key materials in Nigeria</cite> <cite id="0b969edb-0">Procurement data scraping produces ML/NLP-ready datasets for procurement analytics</cite> <cite id="92c75a8e-2">AI risk analytics improve detection and support financial stability in Greater Kampala</cite> <cite id="3f5299e5-2">Blockchain frameworks enable traceability and compliance across multi-party networks</cite>. 
- Remaining gaps include standardized, city-spanning datasets (especially for aggregates), NLP/CV adapted to local languages and informal channels, rigorous pilots quantifying compliance, payment, and carbon benefits, and institutional readiness (skills, policy, governance). <cite id="92c75a8e-0">Limited empirical validation and fragmented data constrain practical diffusion</cite> <cite id="e1bdf674-4">Aggregate-price forecasting lacks local benchmarks despite economic importance</cite> <cite id="0b969edb-1">Kenyan NLP resource gaps hinder integration of local communications</cite> <cite id="3f5299e5-4">Digitalization and socio-political barriers in Nigeria impede blockchain adoption</cite>. Addressing these gaps requires coordinated data, model, governance, and ecosystem interventions tailored to SSA urban construction supply chains. </answer>

Title: Artificial Intelligence in Construction Supply Chains: A Scientometric Review and Future Research Agenda
Snippet: Despite growing interest in artificial intelligence (AI) applications in the construction industry, the literature still lacks a consolidated understanding of how AI functions across the full spectrum of construction supply chain processes. Existing studies are dispersed across different technologies, project stages, and application contexts, making it difficult to identify the intellectual structure of this field, the main areas of AI application, and the barriers that continue to constrain practical implementation. To address this gap, this study conducts a systematic review of AI applications in construction supply chains by combining scientometric analysis with qualitative content synthesis. A total of 212 journal articles retrieved from Scopus were analyzed using VOSviewer-based scientometric analysis and qualitative content synthesis. The scientometric analysis maps annual publication trends, keyword co-occurrence patterns, co-cited sources, influential documents, and collaboration networks. The qualitative synthesis further examines how AI supports construction supply chain management across three broad themes: procurement and production optimization, logistics and material management, and collaborative decision-making for resilience and sustainability. The findings show that AI has been primarily applied to demand forecasting, resource optimization, logistics coordination, contract and document processing, computer vision-based monitoring, and multi-agent decision support. However, its practical diffusion remains constrained by fragmented and low-quality data, limited empirical validation, high implementation costs, algorithmic opacity, cybersecurity risks, and unresolved governance and liability issues. Based on these findings, this study proposes a data-centric and phased research agenda that emphasizes benchmark datasets, human–AI collaboration, lifecycle economic evaluation, explainable AI, and multi-stakeholder governance. The study contributes to the literature by integrating fragmented AI-related research into a structured knowledge map and by clarifying future pathways for developing intelligent, transparent, and resilient construction supply chains.

Title: Optimizing construction supply chains through AI: Streamlining material procurement and logistics for project success
Snippet: The construction industry faces numerous challenges in achieving efficient supply chains, particularly in material procurement and logistics. This paper explores the transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in addressing these challenges and enhancing project success. The discussion covers current issues in construction supply chains, the pivotal role of AI in revolutionizing material procurement and logistics, and practical strategies for implementation. The paper delves into the fragmented communication, inefficient procurement processes, and limited logistics visibility that hinder construction supply chains. AI's application is examined in real-time data analytics, automation of procurement workflows, and the integration of intelligent logistics management systems. The implementation of AI in material procurement includes demand forecasting, automated vendor selection, and order tracking, while logistics streamlining encompasses real-time tracking, route optimization, and proactive delay management. Benefits of AI implementation are highlighted, including cost reduction through waste minimization and optimized logistics, increased efficiency in procurement processes, and improved project timelines. The paper incorporates case studies illustrating successful AI implementation in construction supply chains, showcasing tangible improvements in material procurement and logistics. Despite the evident benefits, the paper acknowledges challenges and considerations in AI adoption within the construction industry. Barriers to implementation are discussed, along with strategies to overcome resistance and ensure successful integration. By streamlining material procurement and logistics through AI, construction projects can achieve heightened efficiency, reduced costs, and improved collaboration among stakeholders, ultimately contributing to overall project success.

Title: Financial Risk Management and Financial Performance of Construction Companies in Greater Kampala Metropolitan Area
Snippet: Studies from African contexts, including Kenya, demonstrate that early detection of supply chain and construction risks helps avert material shortages, labour disruptions, and contractual penalties, thereby improving financial outcomes (Ji et al., 2022). Li et al. (2024) further showed that industrialized and prefabricated construction benefits from formalized risk assessment systems that enhance both operational reliability and economic efficiency. Collectively, these studies underline that comprehensive identification of risks supports the overall financial performance of construction firms, with proactive identification acting as a key driver of financial stability and profitability. Nevertheless, empirical evidence on technology-driven risk identification and its financial implications remains limited in Sub-Saharan African construction contexts. 

Artificial intelligence has become a pivotal tool in risk identification due to its capacity to enhance prediction accuracy and support decision-making processes (Wang, 2024). Salamai et al. (2021) proposed dynamic voting classifiers in supply chain environments for real-time identification of risks, demonstrating that AI improves detection speed and reduces human error, leading to more reliable financial outcomes. Bahamid et al. (2022) also showed that AI-driven systems integrate historical data, market trends, and operational variables to continuously update risk conditions, enabling managers to readjust resources and project plans to avoid losses. El-Sayegh et al. (2021) identified that combining traditional risk identification approaches with AI analytics strengthens the early detection of threats and improves response effectiveness. Yousri et al. (2023) further highlighted that firms utilizing AI in risk identification outperform competitors in budget control, project completion time, and profitability. These findings demonstrate that risk identification through conventional and AI-enhanced systems remains a key mechanism through which construction companies protect financial performance, reduce exposure to uncertainties, and ensure project sustainability. However, little is known about the adoption and effectiveness of AI-enabled risk identification systems in improving financial performance among construction companies in Uganda.

Title: AI in supply chain optimization: A comparative review of USA and African Trends
Snippet: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become increasingly significant in supply chain optimization due to its potential to enhance resilience, performance, and risk management (Modgil et al., 2021;Olan et al., 2022). The global trends in AI adoption in supply chain management indicate a growing interest in leveraging AI technologies to address challenges and improve transparency and traceability, particularly in the food supply chains (Dora et al., 2021). The adoption of AI in supply chain management is still in its early stages, with promising opportunities to elevate supply chain performance (Paul et al., 2022). 

The purpose of the comparative review is to understand the current state of AI integration in the United States and analyze emerging trends and challenges in African countries. This includes exploring potential areas for collaboration and improvement. The study aims to learn from the experiences of AI adoption in the US and apply these insights to the African context. Additionally, it seeks to identify unique challenges and opportunities in African supply chains to develop tailored strategies for AI integration. By comparing the two regions, the review aims to facilitate knowledge sharing and collaboration to enhance supply chain optimization through AI technologies. 

The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in supply chain management has become a focal point for researchers and practitioners due to its potential to revolutionize operational efficiency, resilience, and sustainability. AI technologies offer advanced capabilities for data analysis, decision-making, and optimization, thereby transforming traditional supply chain practices (Mohsen, 2023). The impact of AI on supply chain management performance has been widely acknowledged, with studies highlighting its role in enhancing supply chain resilience, firm performance, and digital transformation (Mohsen, 2023;Modgil et al., 2021;Sullivan & Wamba, 2022). Furthermore, AI-driven innovations have been identified as crucial for improving supply chain finance and sustainability, particularly in industries such as food and drink (Olan et al., 2021;Pawlicka & Bal, 2022). 

The application of AI in supply chain management extends beyond performance enhancement, with studies emphasizing its role in quality enhancement, fraud prediction, and resilience analytics within supply chains (Tang & Lau, 2009;Lokanan & Maddhesia, 2022;Goodarzian et al., 2021).

Title: Addressing the challenges towards the adoption of digital technologies in construction supply chain management
Snippet: This research provides valuable insights into the digital transformation of construction supply chain management. It shed light on the challenges faced by the construction industry in adopting digital technologies in supply chain management. Despite the potential benefits of digital tools, the industry has encountered obstacles such as insufficient training and skills, lack of government support and policies, initial setup complexities, shortage of skilled personnel, and perceived technological complexity. These challenges have significant impacts on supply chain management, these include but not limited to increased costs, reduced productivity, and limited real-time insights into supply chain processes. 

However, the study also highlighted strategies for addressing these challenges and enhancing the adoption of digital technologies in construction supply management in Nigeria. These strategies include improving technical expertise through training, fostering government policies to support digital adoption, promoting awareness, simplifying technology interfaces, and leveraging real-time data for better decision-making. The findings in this study should be interpreted with caution for the fact that the subjective factors of the experts consulted could have influenced their responses. To validate these findings, future research that employs a more diverse pool of experts and or objective approach should be considered. could validate the findings in this study. Additionally, in-depth Future research can focus on in-depth analysis of the potential impact of emerging technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Blockchain on construction supply chain management could be a point of focus.

Based on these findings, this study proposes a data-centric and phased research agenda that emphasizes benchmark datasets, human–AI collaboration, lifecycle economic evaluation, explainable AI, and multi-stakeholder governance. The study contributes to the literature by integrating fragmented AI-related research into a structured knowledge map and by clarifying future pathways for developing intelligent, transparent, and resilient construction supply chains.

documents.title: Optimizing construction supply chains through AI: Streamlining material procurement and logistics for project success
documents.snippet: The construction industry faces numerous challenges in achieving efficient supply chains, particularly in material procurement and logistics. This paper explores the transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in addressing these challenges and enhancing project success. The discussion covers current issues in construction supply chains, the pivotal role of AI in revolutionizing material procurement and logistics, and practical strategies for implementation. The paper delves into the fragmented communication, inefficient procurement processes, and limited logistics visibility that hinder construction supply chains. AI's application is examined in real-time data analytics, automation of procurement workflows, and the integration of intelligent logistics management systems. The implementation of AI in material procurement includes demand forecasting, automated vendor selection, and order tracking, while logistics streamlining encompasses real-time tracking, route optimization, and proactive delay management. Benefits of AI implementation are highlighted, including cost reduction through waste minimization and optimized logistics, increased efficiency in procurement processes, and improved project timelines. The paper incorporates case studies illustrating successful AI implementation in construction supply chains, showcasing tangible improvements in material procurement and logistics. Despite the evident benefits, the paper acknowledges challenges and considerations in AI adoption within the construction industry. Barriers to implementation are discussed, along with strategies to overcome resistance and ensure successful integration. By streamlining material procurement and logistics through AI, construction projects can achieve heightened efficiency, reduced costs, and improved collaboration among stakeholders, ultimately contributing to overall project success.

documents.title: Financial Risk Management and Financial Performance of Construction Companies in Greater Kampala Metropolitan Area
documents.snippet:
Studies from African contexts, including Kenya, demonstrate that early detection of supply chain and construction risks helps avert material shortages, labour disruptions, and contractual penalties, thereby improving financial outcomes (Ji et al., 2022). Li et al. (2024) further showed that industrialized and prefabricated construction benefits from formalized risk assessment systems that enhance both operational reliability and economic efficiency. Collectively, these studies underline that comprehensive identification of risks supports the overall financial performance of construction firms, with proactive identification acting as a key driver of financial stability and profitability. Nevertheless, empirical evidence on technology-driven risk identification and its financial implications remains limited in Sub-Saharan African construction contexts. 

Artificial intelligence has become a pivotal tool in risk identification due to its capacity to enhance prediction accuracy and support decision-making processes (Wang, 2024). Salamai et al. (2021) proposed dynamic voting classifiers in supply chain environments for real-time identification of risks, demonstrating that AI improves detection speed and reduces human error, leading to more reliable financial outcomes. Bahamid et al. (2022) also showed that AI-driven systems integrate historical data, market trends, and operational variables to continuously update risk conditions, enabling managers to readjust resources and project plans to avoid losses. El-Sayegh et al. (2021) identified that combining traditional risk identification approaches with AI analytics strengthens the early detection of threats and improves response effectiveness. Yousri et al. (2023) further highlighted that firms utilizing AI in risk identification outperform competitors in budget control, project completion time, and profitability. These findings demonstrate that risk identification through conventional and AI-enhanced systems remains a key mechanism through which construction companies protect financial performance, reduce exposure to uncertainties, and ensure project sustainability. However, little is known about the adoption and effectiveness of AI-enabled risk identification systems in improving financial performance among construction companies in Uganda.

documents.title: AI in supply chain optimization: A comparative review of USA and African Trends
documents.snippet:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become increasingly significant in supply chain optimization due to its potential to enhance resilience, performance, and risk management (Modgil et al., 2021;Olan et al., 2022). The global trends in AI adoption in supply chain management indicate a growing interest in leveraging AI technologies to address challenges and improve transparency and traceability, particularly in the food supply chains (Dora et al., 2021). The adoption of AI in supply chain management is still in its early stages, with promising opportunities to elevate supply chain performance (Paul et al., 2022). 

The purpose of the comparative review is to understand the current state of AI integration in the United States and analyze emerging trends and challenges in African countries. This includes exploring potential areas for collaboration and improvement. The study aims to learn from the experiences of AI adoption in the US and apply these insights to the African context. Additionally, it seeks to identify unique challenges and opportunities in African supply chains to develop tailored strategies for AI integration. By comparing the two regions, the review aims to facilitate knowledge sharing and collaboration to enhance supply chain optimization through AI technologies. 

The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in supply chain management has become a focal point for researchers and practitioners due to its potential to revolutionize operational efficiency, resilience, and sustainability. AI technologies offer advanced capabilities for data analysis, decision-making, and optimization, thereby transforming traditional supply chain practices (Mohsen, 2023). The impact of AI on supply chain management performance has been widely acknowledged, with studies highlighting its role in enhancing supply chain resilience, firm performance, and digital transformation (Mohsen, 2023;Modgil et al., 2021;Sullivan & Wamba, 2022). Furthermore, AI-driven innovations have been identified as crucial for improving supply chain finance and sustainability, particularly in industries such as food and drink (Olan et al., 2021;Pawlicka & Bal, 2022). 

The application of AI in supply chain management extends beyond performance enhancement, with studies emphasizing its role in quality enhancement, fraud prediction, and resilience analytics within supply chains (Tang & Lau, 2009;Lokanan & Maddhesia, 2022;Goodarzian et al., 2021).

documents.title: Addressing the challenges towards the adoption of digital technologies in construction supply chain management
documents.snippet:
This research provides valuable insights into the digital transformation of construction supply chain management. It shed light on the challenges faced by the construction industry in adopting digital technologies in supply chain management. Despite the potential benefits of digital tools, the industry has encountered obstacles such as insufficient training and skills, lack of government support and policies, initial setup complexities, shortage of skilled personnel, and perceived technological complexity. These challenges have significant impacts on supply chain management, these include but not limited to increased costs, reduced productivity, and limited real-time insights into supply chain processes. 

However, the study also highlighted strategies for addressing these challenges and enhancing the adoption of digital technologies in construction supply management in Nigeria. These strategies include improving technical expertise through training, fostering government policies to support digital adoption, promoting awareness, simplifying technology interfaces, and leveraging real-time data for better decision-making. The findings in this study should be interpreted with caution for the fact that the subjective factors of the experts consulted could have influenced their responses. Title: Identification of Aggregates Quarries via Computer Vision Analysis as a Tool for Sustainable Aggregates Management and Land Planning
Snippet: The mineral raw materials industry is crucial for European industry, with the European Economic and Social Committee estimating that 70% of the industry relies directly or indirectly on its supply. In the context of a decarbonized and digitalized economy, the new European industrial model requires carbon-neutral raw materials and production processes. The crucial role of aggregates mining, as the primary construction material, emerges as a key supplier in this paradigm. Aggregates are the main component of the built environment and are a social and economic engine in most countries. Quarries of this type include a wide range of sizes and exploitation methods and use characteristic mining and processing equipment. Quarries are commonly close to their processing plants, which transform natural rock into crushed and ground materials with different grain sizes depending on the future uses. The quarry itself and the presence of certain equipment and facilities help distinguish it from mining sites that exploit other materials. Effective management of aggregates quarries is important in promoting circular economy practices, ensuring efficient management, reuse, and recycling of diverse wastes, including the recovery of high-value components and the production of recycled aggregates, and addressing construction and demolition waste (DCW) management. As aggregates become a progressively scarcer resource due to the increasing demand from developing countries, it is essential to provide reliable and comprehensive information on their potential to the public, policymakers, and other stakeholders to promote their use. This study focuses on employing artificial intelligence and computer vision analysis to automatically identify aggregates quarries from satellite images within continental Spain. A model has been trained to detect aggregates quarries from satellite images by computer vision. The model permits the detection of mining exploitation and the objects located at the interior, which permits determination of the type of mine and the activity status of it. The findings highlight the ability of artificial vision to discern quarries and distinguish whether the observed feature is an aggregates quarry. Additionally, the technology allows for the determination of the quarry’s operational status, distinguishing between active and abandoned quarries. The ability to detect the locations of quarries and assess their activity statuses is of significant value for resource exploration initiatives and location-allocation assessments. It can be a valuable tool for authorities involved in land planning, activities monitoring, and early detection of potential illegal mining activities. Title: Tackling the Data Sourcing Problem in Construction Procurement Using File-Scraping Algorithms
Snippet: : The Architecture, Engineering and Construction (AEC) sector has a lower adoption rate of machine learning (ML) tools than other industries with similar characteristics. A signiﬁcant contributing factor to this lower adoption rate is the limited availability of data, as ML techniques rely on large datasets to train algorithms effectively. However, the construction process generates substantial data that provide detailed characterisation of a project. In this regard, this paper presents a data-scraping algorithm to search construction procurement repositories systematically to develop an ML-ready dataset for training data for ML and natural language processing (NLP) algorithms focused on con-struction’s procurement phase. This tool automatically scrapes procurement repositories, developing a procurement ﬁle dataset comprisfﬁng bills of quantities (BoQs) and project speciﬁcations.

Title: State of NLP in Kenya: A Survey
Snippet: Kenya, known for its linguistic diversity, faces unique challenges and promising opportunities in advancing Natural Language Processing (NLP) technologies, particularly for its underrepresented indigenous languages. This survey provides a detailed assessment of the current state of NLP in Kenya, emphasizing ongoing efforts in dataset creation, machine translation, sentiment analysis, and speech recognition for local dialects such as Kiswahili, Dholuo, Kikuyu, and Luhya. Despite these advancements, the development of NLP in Kenya remains constrained by limited resources and tools, resulting in the underrepresentation of most indigenous languages in digital spaces. This paper uncovers significant gaps by critically evaluating the available datasets and existing NLP models, most notably the need for large-scale language models and the insufficient digital representation of Indigenous languages. We also analyze key NLP applications: machine translation, information retrieval, and sentiment analysis-examining how they are tailored to address local linguistic needs. Furthermore, the paper explores the governance, policies, and regulations shaping the future of AI and NLP in Kenya and proposes a strategic roadmap to guide future research and development efforts. Our goal is to provide a foundation for accelerating the growth of NLP technologies that meet Kenya's diverse linguistic demands.

Title: State of NLP in Kenya: A Survey
Snippet: While the field of NLP is very broad and keeps growing, we aim to cover as many subtopics are possible. 

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows; first, we look at similar surveys and works in Section 2. In Section 4 , we survey all datasets on Kenyan languages. In section 5 we survey NLP applications developed in Kenya or using kenyan languages. We touch on categories of applications such as machine translations, information retrieval, and text classification. In section 6 we look at governance, policies and regulations related to AI and NLP specifically. We highlight different efforts by governments and communities to draft AI policies and regulations around the technology. Finally in section 8 we discuss a possible roadmap for NLP research in Kenya.

Title: Building Corpora for Low-Resource Kenyan Languages
Snippet: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has become a vital component of modern artificial intelligence (AI), shaping various sectors from healthcare to commerce. In recent years, advances in hardware, sophisticated algorithms, and the availability of large text data sets have enabled NLP systems to deliver unprecedented capabilities, transforming many aspects of human activity (Chollet, 2021). Generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT, exemplify the reach and impact of NLP innovations. However, these advances have exacerbated the global digital divide, particularly in linguistic terms. Many African languages, including those indigenous to Kenya, remain excluded from these developments, limiting access to critical information and technological benefits for their speakers (Nekoto et al., 2020). 

The linguistic divide is rooted in historical inequalities that stem from colonialism, which imposed foreign languages such as English, French, and Portuguese as the official means of communication in Africa. These languages dominate education, governance, and technology, often at the expense of indigenous languages (Bamgbose, 2011). Language policies in education, while sometimes supportive of mother-tongue instruction on paper, often lack practical implementation mechanisms (Awuor, 2019). This legacy has led to the marginalisation of a large part of the African population, who do not speak these colonial languages fluently, restricting their access to essential information and the technological tools developed for those languages (Nduati, 2016). During the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, critical public health information in Kenya was predominantly disseminated in English and Kiswahili, excluding speakers of indigenous languages, especially in rural areas. 

This linguistic exclusion underscores the urgent need to integrate African languages into AI and NLP technologies. Building high-quality linguistic corpora for underrepresented languages is crucial to enable language technologies such as machine translation, speech recognition, and speech synthesis for African languages. In this context, our project focused on developing language corpora for the three Kenyan languages Kidaw'ida, Kalenjin, and Dholuo, by collecting text and speech data and translating the text data into Kiswahili to generate parallel corpora. These resources are intended to facilitate the development of NLP applications that meet the needs of African communities, thereby promoting linguistic diversity in AI development.

Title: Tackling the Data Sourcing Problem in Construction Procurement Using File-Scraping Algorithms
Snippet: In recent years, there has been increased interest in implementing ML and NLP tools in the AEC sector [1,2]. Still, the adoption rate of these tools is low compared to other industries with similar characteristics [3]. 

A significant contributing factor to this lower adoption rate is the limited availability of data, as ML techniques rely on large datasets to train algorithms effectively [4,5]. This difficulty in sourcing abundant data in the construction sector represents one of the main challenges for ML developers within the AEC industry [6,7]. Nonetheless, this paradigm clashes with the inherent workings of the construction process since it generates a significant amount of data that offer comprehensive characterisation of a project [4,8]. 

In the specific case of Portuguese Construction Procurement, public construction projects are mandatorily submitted to online, open-source repositories [9,10]. However, the consultation and extraction of procurement files is decentralised and not automated, making data agglomeration difficult and time-consuming [11]. Previous studies have tackled this difficulty by scraping procurement data in these repositories to a tabular dataset to be used in ML applications [11,12]. Thus, if the necessary diligence is ensured, the procurement phase represents a great opportunity for data aggregation. 

In light of this, this paper presents a data-scraping algorithm capable of extracting data from construction procurement repositories. This tool automatically scrapes procurement repositories, developing a procurement file dataset comprising BoQs and project specifications. Future studies will use the gathered data to develop an ML-ready dataset for training data for ML, and NLP algorithms focused on construction's procurement phase. 

The remainder of this document is organised into three sections: Section 2 presents the methods and codes developed to scrape open-source data to a semi-structured format; Section 3 describes the gathered data and briefly highlights the framework where scraped data will be used; and Section 4 presents our conclusions and final remarks.

documents.title: State of NLP in Kenya: A Survey
documents.snippet: Kenya, known for its linguistic diversity, faces unique challenges and promising opportunities in advancing Natural Language Processing (NLP) technologies, particularly for its underrepresented indigenous languages. This survey provides a detailed assessment of the current state of NLP in Kenya, emphasizing ongoing efforts in dataset creation, machine translation, sentiment analysis, and speech recognition for local dialects such as Kiswahili, Dholuo, Kikuyu, and Luhya. Despite these advancements, the development of NLP in Kenya remains constrained by limited resources and tools, resulting in the underrepresentation of most indigenous languages in digital spaces. This paper uncovers significant gaps by critically evaluating the available datasets and existing NLP models, most notably the need for large-scale language models and the insufficient digital representation of Indigenous languages. We also analyze key NLP applications: machine translation, information retrieval, and sentiment analysis-examining how they are tailored to address local linguistic needs. Furthermore, the paper explores the governance, policies, and regulations shaping the future of AI and NLP in Kenya and proposes a strategic roadmap to guide future research and development efforts. Our goal is to provide a foundation for accelerating the growth of NLP technologies that meet Kenya's diverse linguistic demands.

documents.title: Building Corpora for Low-Resource Kenyan Languages
documents.snippet:
Natural Language Processing (NLP) has become a vital component of modern artificial intelligence (AI), shaping various sectors from healthcare to commerce. In recent years, advances in hardware, sophisticated algorithms, and the availability of large text data sets have enabled NLP systems to deliver unprecedented capabilities, transforming many aspects of human activity (Chollet, 2021). Generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT, exemplify the reach and impact of NLP innovations. However, these advances have exacerbated the global digital divide, particularly in linguistic terms. Many African languages, including those indigenous to Kenya, remain excluded from these developments, limiting access to critical information and technological benefits for their speakers (Nekoto et al., 2020). 

The linguistic divide is rooted in historical inequalities that stem from colonialism, which imposed foreign languages such as English, French, and Portuguese as the official means of communication in Africa. These languages dominate education, governance, and technology, often at the expense of indigenous languages (Bamgbose, 2011). Language policies in education, while sometimes supportive of mother-tongue instruction on paper, often lack practical implementation mechanisms (Awuor, 2019). This legacy has led to the marginalisation of a large part of the African population, who do not speak these colonial languages fluently, restricting their access to essential information and the technological tools developed for those languages (Nduati, 2016). During the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, critical public health information in Kenya was predominantly disseminated in English and Kiswahili, excluding speakers of indigenous languages, especially in rural areas. 

This linguistic exclusion underscores the urgent need to integrate African languages into AI and NLP technologies. Building high-quality linguistic corpora for underrepresented languages is crucial to enable language technologies such as machine translation, speech recognition, and speech synthesis for African languages. In this context, our project focused on developing language corpora for the three Kenyan languages Kidaw'ida, Kalenjin, and Dholuo, by collecting text and speech data and translating the text data into Kiswahili to generate parallel corpora. These resources are intended to facilitate the development of NLP applications that meet the needs of African communities, thereby promoting linguistic diversity in AI development.
