In recent years, there has been increased interest in implementing ML and NLP tools in the AEC sector [1,2]. Still, the adoption rate of these tools is low compared to other industries with similar characteristics [3]. 

A significant contributing factor to this lower adoption rate is the limited availability of data, as ML techniques rely on large datasets to train algorithms effectively [4,5]. This difficulty in sourcing abundant data in the construction sector represents one of the main challenges for ML developers within the AEC industry [6,7]. Nonetheless, this paradigm clashes with the inherent workings of the construction process since it generates a significant amount of data that offer comprehensive characterisation of a project [4,8]. 

In the specific case of Portuguese Construction Procurement, public construction projects are mandatorily submitted to online, open-source repositories [9,10]. However, the consultation and extraction of procurement files is decentralised and not automated, making data agglomeration difficult and time-consuming [11]. Previous studies have tackled this difficulty by scraping procurement data in these repositories to a tabular dataset to be used in ML applications [11,12]. Thus, if the necessary diligence is ensured, the procurement phase represents a great opportunity for data aggregation. 

In light of this, this paper presents a data-scraping algorithm capable of extracting data from construction procurement repositories. This tool automatically scrapes procurement repositories, developing a procurement file dataset comprising BoQs and project specifications. Future studies will use the gathered data to develop an ML-ready dataset for training data for ML, and NLP algorithms focused on construction's procurement phase.

Title: IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TECHNOLOGIES ON CONSTRUCTION EFFICIENCY AND SAFETY IN NIGERIA
Snippet: The findings indicate that AI applications significantly contribute to improving project scheduling accuracy, cost estimation, and safety performance on construction sites. However, despite these evident benefits, the adoption rate remains sluggish due to the absence of clear regulatory frameworks, lack of industry-specific AI policies, and limited technical literacy among professionals. The researchers recommend comprehensive policy reforms and the implementation of nationwide AI education and training programs to facilitate broader AI integration in the sector. Their study enriches the current research by demonstrating the practical benefits of AI while emphasizing the regulatory and knowledge-based limitations that must be addressed to foster greater acceptance and usage. Braimah, Ajagbe and Olonade (2024) -Conducted by researchers from the University of Ibadan and the University of Lagos, this 2024 Springer review synthesized ML approaches to predict mechanical properties of sandcrete blocks using quarry dust. Grounded in Nigerian experimental data, the review found that machine learning techniques like regression and classification methods can accurately estimate strength attributes, reducing the need for expansive lab testing. This work emphasizes AI's role in enhancing sustainable local materials, streamlining block production, and promoting environmentally conscious practices. It offers methodological insights for integrating ML into standard material quality assurance processes across local industries. Ahmadu et al. (2023) -Focusing on price prediction, this empirical research used Python-based models Back Propagation Neural Network (BPNN) and an Autoencoder-BPNN hybrid to forecast construction material prices using data from the Nigerian Bureau of Statistics, Central Bank, and vendors. The models achieved high accuracy (82-98%) across materials: the hybrid excelled in predicting reinforcement prices, while plain BPNN was superior for steel and cement. This study provides valuable forecasting (JBER); Journal of January, 2026 Biodiversity and Environmental Research Editions tools, boosting contractors' and quantity surveyors' budgeting accuracy and aiding efficient cash-flow management in volatile markets. It clearly demonstrates AI's strategic role in financial planning for construction projects. Njama-Abang (2025) performed a PRISMA-guided systematic review of global ML applications in construction, with emphasis on the Nigerian context. The review revealed that machine learning enhances project efficiency, cost control, risk prediction, and maintenance scheduling internationally. Specific Nigerian opportunities include resource optimization and predictive equipment maintenance.

Title: Application of machine learning in cement price prediction through a web-based system
Snippet: Hwang et al. [26] observed that as building projects increase in size and the construction period's length is prolonged, there is a need to note construction material prices due to inflation factors. 

This study aims to predict cement prices in the Nigerian construction industry through a machine learning-based approach. Specifically, a web-based learning platform was developed that uses machine learning algorithms on historical data in the form of knowledge management stored by a construction firm to predict future prices of cement products. The purpose is to help the construction firm predict cement prices for their upcoming projects in their bidding and procurement planning procedures. The approach used in this study is built on available historical data and numerical values of factors influencing cement prices. Similarly, Naser [27] used time-series data to predict oil prices in Iraq. This paper contributes to the existing scientific body of knowledge on automating cement price prediction using machine learning.

Title: Application of machine learning in cement price prediction through a web-based system
Snippet: According to [28], [29], building materials used in the construction industry represent one of the most important factors affecting its successful performance. This makes the building construction sector a significant contributor to the construction industry's effectiveness primarily due to the associated cost in procuring them [12], [30]. One of such building materials that are crucial to the construction industry is cement. The need for growth and development spurs the construction industry due to the continuous inflow of investment from different stakeholders it creates a high demand for cement products. This is Nigeria's case, a growing economy due to the new construction projects in housing and heavy civil construction that spring up daily. Ugochukwu et al. [30] noted that the demand for cement thrives in this kind of economies. Velumani and Nampoothiri [23] reported that the fluctuation in cement prices affects the construction industry's performance. Therefore, cement price prediction has taken center stage in the construction industry [23]. 

Several studies have pointed to the direction this paper aims to achieve to predict construction material prices. The study by Marzouk and Amin [21] used fuzzy logic and neural networks to predict the changes in building materials prices. Their system helps identify construction materials susceptible to changes that may affect contract price and expect future material cost changes. The primary data used were the changes in the material prices in the Egyptian construction market within a space of 10 years. The study by Issa [24] used artificial neural networks (ANN) to predict future construction material prices using the contractor's past costs of procured building materials and the conditions influencing these building materials. To forecast construction material prices, Hwang et al. [26] developed an automated time-series material cost forecasting (ATMF) system that uses the Box-Jenkins approach to produce a best-fitting model and forecast values for the construction material prices. The ATMF system developed by Hwang et al. [26] can help decision-makers in the construction sector predict future trends in construction material costs. Lee et al. [31] used a multivariate time series analysis to predict the prices of iron ore, a raw material in the production of steel products used in the construction industry. In predicting iron ore prices, system expected more than 2.3 times the past average values in previous studies.

Title: Comparative Evaluation of Statistical, Machine‐Learning, and Deep‐Learning Models for Construction Sand and Gravel Price Forecasting: A Synthetic‐Data, Simulation‐Based Benchmark
Snippet: regional level are shaped by local quarrying regulations, hydrology cycles, and infrastructure investment pipelines, which are structurally distinct from mainstream commodity markets such as crude oil or copper. For project owners, contractors, and ready-mix concrete producers, even modest miscalibrations of expected aggregate prices can propagate into significant cost overruns, because aggregates typically account for 60% -75% of concrete mass and a nontrivial share of total project material cost. Reliable monthly price forecasting therefore has direct economic value. 

Despite its practical importance, aggregate-price forecasting has received considerably less attention in the quantitative-modeling literature than mainstream commodities such as crude oil, copper, or steel. The steel-price literature, for instance, now encompasses a substantial body of machine-learning benchmarks for regional Chinese markets, drawing on Gaussian process regression (GPR), neural networks, and tree-based ensembles [ 2 -5]. Analogous work for base metals such as copper has explored Random Forest (RF) and decision-tree variants [ 6]. In the construction sector, machine-learning approaches have been applied to cement price prediction [ 7], building material cost indices [ 8,9], and general construction cost estimation [ 10 -12]. Yet no peer-reviewed study, to the authors' knowledge, has conducted a rigorous multimethod quantitative benchmark specifically for regional construction aggregate (sand and gravel) prices. This gap is consequential: aggregate markets are structurally different from metals or energy commodities in that price formation is overwhelmingly local, transport costs are high relative to product value, and supply is subject to discrete regulatory shocks (e.g., river-sand extraction bans) rather than to global macroeconomic drivers. 

Several factors complicate aggregate price forecasting. First, markets are strongly regional: price signals observed in one city provide limited information about another city even within the same province. Second, time series at the regional monthly resolution are typically short -often only 3 -5 years of usable data -because consistent reporting practices are recent. Third, multiple structurally related drivers are usually available (production, inventory, costs, downstream concrete price, etc.), creating moderate-dimensional regression problems with substantial multicollinearity.

attempts.answer:
Summary answer
- Short answer: AI-driven digital integration of construction material supply chains can substantially reduce, but not reliably eliminate, price volatility in Addis Ababa’s informal markets. Mechanism-based and empirical studies show that integrated data, predictive analytics, and connected logistics enable earlier warning of disruptions, more accurate demand/supply forecasts, and proactive procurement and routing that moderate spikes and shortages. In Ethiopia and similar LMIC contexts, digitized price data and platform integrations have improved forecasting accuracy and supported adaptive contracting and procurement; however, structural features of Addis Ababa’s markets—deep informality, shortages of key items, and regulatory frictions—mean platform-only solutions are unlikely to fully stabilize prices without complementary reforms and infrastructure. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-0">AI-driven predictive analytics can forecast movements in key construction materials (steel, concrete, lumber) and warn of disruptions (e.g., factory shutdowns, shipping slowdowns), enabling early procurement or delay decisions that directly mitigate volatility exposure</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-1">AI-enabled procurement and logistics (demand forecasting, automated vendor selection, real-time tracking, route optimization) cut waste, reduce costs, and improve continuity, which dampen volatility-driven overruns</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Predictive analytics improves forecast accuracy by 20–50%, reduces inventory volatility, and moderates price spikes by preventing panic reactions and enabling alternative sourcing and safety-stock adjustments</cite> <cite id="da55d358-0">Time-series models (ARIMA, multiple regression) for construction material prices in Egypt achieved 1.4–2.8% MAPE, demonstrating that accurate forecasting is feasible to support better budgeting under price swings</cite> <cite id="da55d358-4">A Nigeria dataset integrating supplier surveys and online marketplace data feeds into LSTM price prediction and procurement optimization, with proposed API and blockchain integrations for real-time pricing and transparency to address regional price disparities</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-4">AI-driven analytics help identify market trends early, minimizing financial impact of short-term volatility via early procurement, bulk buying, and escalation clauses</cite>.

- Evidence in Ethiopia/Addis Ababa: The city’s construction ecosystem is shaped by informality, regulation, and chronic shortages (e.g., corrugated iron, concrete slabs), which heighten sensitivity to logistics and policy shocks; yet large-scale investments (e.g., Dangote cement) have pushed cement prices down from >500 to <250 birr, indicating that supply-side capacity expansion can meaningfully dampen price levels and swings. However, informality and land speculation dominate land and housing markets, implying persistent frictions that can transmit shocks to material markets. <cite id="c85950f1-0">Ethiopia’s cement sector saw prices fall from 500 birr+ to under 250 birr after Dangote’s large plant, illustrating supply expansion’s stabilizing effect on prices</cite> <cite id="c85950f1-3">Addis Ababa exhibits many half-finished buildings and chronic shortages of common materials (corrugated iron, reinforced concrete slabs), with tight regulations and a shortage of construction equipment and financing contributing to delays and cost volatility</cite> <cite id="c85950f1-3">The government regulates material prices and construction equipment access, reinforcing that policy and logistics constraints, not only market forces, drive volatility</cite> <cite id="193dc8e6-4">In Ethiopia, about three-quarters of urban land supply in major cities flows through informal markets due to formal market inefficiencies and speculation, which contributes to high and unstable land and construction costs</cite>.

- What refutes “eliminate”: Multiple studies and Addis Ababa’s institutional context show that volatility stems from macro shocks, geopolitics, energy/fuel costs, supply chain disruptions, and structural informality/speculation; digital integration reduces exposure but cannot remove these structural drivers absent broader reforms. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-2">Supply chain disruptions, geopolitical instability, and inflation are primary drivers of material price volatility, causing overruns, delays, and disputes, necessitating proactive risk mitigation</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-0">Early warning of shipping delays, factory shutdowns, and geopolitical unrest via AI enables mitigation, but such shocks are external and recurrent</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Improved forecasting reduces panic-driven reactions and stockouts, but volatility persists when disruptions propagate across networks</cite> <cite id="193dc8e6-0">Ethiopian urban grain market studies find no clear difference in volatility across markets, with trends rising—suggesting persistence even when information flows integrate</cite> <cite id="193dc8e6-4">Informal land/speculative markets keep supply tight and prices elevated, making volatility hard to eradicate by ICT alone</cite>.

Mechanisms by which digital/AI integration can reduce volatility
- Early warning and disruption analytics: AI over ERP/WMS/TMS data (customs, sensors, GPS, e-commerce) detects supplier distress, transport delays, and geopolitical shocks that propagate into material price spikes, enabling rerouting, alternative sourcing, and inventory adjustments. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-0">Monitoring for strikes, shipping slowdowns, and factory shutdowns lets contractors procure alternatives or adjust timing to avoid spikes</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Predictive systems with ML detect demand surges and transport delays (e.g., extreme weather, geopolitics), allowing pre-emptive rerouting and sourcing that prevent panic buying and stabilize prices</cite>.
- Demand/supply forecasting and procurement optimization: Machine learning on historical and real-time data improves forecast accuracy, supports dynamic purchasing windows, and integrates with BIM and ERP for rolling budget updates. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-1">Demand forecasting, automated vendor selection, and order tracking reduce procurement cycle waste and costs</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-4">AI-driven analytics spot market trends early so early procurement or flexible escalation clauses minimize financial impact of short-term surges</cite> <cite id="da55d358-0">ARIMA and regression models achieved 1.4–2.8% MAPE for steel, cement, brick, ceramic, gravel in Egypt, enabling tighter budgeting under volatility</cite> <cite id="da55d358-2">Integrating monthly price bulletins into automated cost workflows enabled real-time budget adjustments during 101% cement and 134% steel increases (2021–2023), showing feasibility of adaptive frameworks</cite>.
- Logistics continuity and inventory smoothing: Real-time tracking, route optimization, and digital twins simulate disruptions and adjust safety stocks, reducing service interruptions and procurement premiums. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-1">Real-time logistics visibility and proactive delay management streamline flows and reduce costs</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">AI forecasting improves by 20–50%, lowers inventory volatility, and predictive models cut procurement premiums by maintaining continuity and preventing panic-driven price hikes</cite>.
- Data ecosystems and transparency: Aggregating supplier reports, marketplace prices, and macro indicators into unified platforms improves price discovery and reduces regional disparities; proposed Blockchain/APIs further ensure timely updates and auditability. <cite id="da55d358-4">A Nigeria dataset compiles supplier and online marketplace prices, integrates them into LSTM forecasting within a procurement system (BuildCES), and proposes API and blockchain to deliver real-time, transparent pricing and reduce regional disparities</cite>.

Evidence from Ethiopia and Addis Ababa: feasibility and limits
- Ethiopia’s cement example shows large swings can be countered by supply-side capacity and data-driven procurement strategies. <cite id="c85950f1-0">After Dangote’s plant, cement prices fell from 500+ to under 250 birr, directly cutting a major input’s volatility footprint and benefiting housing projects</cite>. This suggests digital integration layered on top of expanded capacity can stabilize prices more broadly.
- However, Addis Ababa’s regulatory environment and shortages create frictions that transmit shocks. <cite id="c85950f1-3">Shortages of corrugated iron and reinforced concrete slabs and high costs of capital equipment cause delays and cost volatility</cite> <cite id="c85950f1-3">Price and equipment regulation, short-term high-interest lending, and large share of owner-finance lead to underbuilding and sensitivity to input shocks</cite>. Informality and speculation in land/real estate mean housing and materials demand remain volatile. <cite id="193dc8e6-4">About 75% of land in major Ethiopian cities is supplied via informal channels—driven by formal market failures—contributing to high and speculative land prices that ripple into construction costs</cite>.
- Evidence from Addis Ababa’s construction sites shows that despite appearances of a boom, chronic material deficits persist, indicating structural supply and logistics issues beyond what ICT can fix alone. <cite id="c85950f1-3">Many half-finished buildings and persistent shortages point to supply-chain and logistics bottlenecks, not only demand-side volatility</cite>.

Evidence from LMIC construction markets on digital mitigation of volatility
- Forecasting precision and decision support: <cite id="da55d358-0">Egypt models achieved 1.4–2.8% MAPE for five key materials, supporting better budgeting and reducing over/underestimation errors</cite> <cite id="da55d358-2">A seven-governorate residential build-inventory case integrated monthly price bulletins into cost workflows to perform real-time budget adjustments amid 101% cement and 134% steel increases (2021–2023)</cite>. These show digitalized price monitoring and adaptive workflows can hedge volatility effectively.
- Data-driven procurement platforms: <cite id="da55d358-4">Nigeria’s Building Materials Dataset integrates supplier surveys and online marketplace data, feeds an LSTM-based estimator in BuildCES, and proposes API and blockchain for real-time price updates and transparency to address regional price disparities</cite>. This architecture directly targets volatility drivers (delayed info, regional asymmetries) and supports dynamic procurement.
- Macro-infrastructure linkages: <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Digital integration of customs, logistics, and market data reduces stockouts and procurement premiums, moderating crisis-period price increases</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-1">Automated workflows and real-time tracking reduce waste and improve efficiency, lowering cost variance exposure</cite>.

This reinforces that digital monitoring and analytics are key mitigants, but not panaceas.

Evidence that can refute over-optimism
- Structural volatility sources: <cite id="7ee6d9c7-2">Supply chain disruptions, geopolitical instability, and inflation remain principal drivers of material price volatility, causing overruns and disputes</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-0">AI can only anticipate some shocks (e.g., factory shutdowns, shipping slowdowns); unpredictable geopolitical events can overwhelm localized analytics</cite>.
- Market power and platformization: While not Ethiopia-specific, digitalization can create new concentration risks (e.g., dominant platforms, data monopolies) that suppress competition and sustain price dispersion; absent antitrust and open-data mandates, digital integration may not lower prices for informal actors. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-1">Fragmented communication and limited visibility are core frictions; integration depends on stakeholder collaboration and data sharing, which can be blocked by incumbents</cite>.
- Infrastructure constraints: Digital gains require reliable energy, connectivity, and trusted data flows; in Ethiopian urban peripheries, logistics and payment frictions persist. <cite id="c85950f1-3">Shortages and equipment constraints slow delivery even when orders are placed</cite> <cite id="da55d358-4">Regional price disparities persist, motivating API-driven real-time updates and transparency to correct asymmetries</cite>.
- Informality and speculation: <cite id="193dc8e6-4">Three-quarters of land supply in major Ethiopian cities flows through informal channels, with speculation and hoarding inflating prices and making markets brittle to information shocks</cite>. Digital platforms may not reach unbanked, small traders without mobile money and regulatory support.

What would further support or refute the claim
- Field experiments in Addis Ababa: A randomized rollout of an integrated platform for cement, sand, and bricks linking mini-markets, wholesalers, and transporters with real-time price feeds, predictive alerts, and mobile money payments, measuring changes in price dispersion and short-run volatility versus control sites. <cite id="da55d358-4">API-integrated real-time price updates and blockchain-audited transactions are proposed to reduce disparities and fraud</cite>.
- Quasi-experimental expansion of state or port/customs digitization in Ethiopia: Measuring post-digitization reductions in delivery times and price premiums for construction inputs, controlling for macro shocks. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Improved responsiveness moderates price increases during crises by maintaining supply continuity</cite>.
- Inclusion mandates: Studies assessing effects of open data portals or mandated API sharing with small suppliers on price stability and trader revenues. <cite id="da55d358-4">Open, integrated data ecosystems reduce regional price disparities and enable procurement optimization</cite>.

Practical pathway for Addis Ababa
- Anchor with infrastructure: Expand metered electricity and LTE/5G coverage to mini-markets and transport nodes; pair with affordable mobile data plans for traders. <cite id="da55d358-4">Real-time APIs and geospatial mapping are needed to correct regional disparities</cite>.
- Build an Addis Ababa Construction Materials Data Commons: Aggregate daily prices from 50+ traders/wholesalers via structured SMS/API, integrate port/customs/duty and fuel indices, and publish open dashboards. <cite id="da55d358-4">A structured time-series dataset of suppliers and online marketplaces enables forecasting and procurement optimization</cite>.
- Platform features: 
  - Predictive early-warning panel (steel, cement, sand, bricks) with procurement recommendations and vendor network routing. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-0">Forecasting and disruption warnings guide early buy vs. delay decisions</cite>.
  - Dynamic escalation/contingency clauses and rolling budgets tied to market indices, implemented in BIM/ERP. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-4">Escalation clauses and early trend detection reduce financial impact</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-1">ERP-BIM integration supports rolling cost updates</cite>.
  - Logistics optimization and vehicle routing with real-time rerouting for duty-free corridors. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-1">Route optimization and proactive delay management reduce costs</cite>.
- Governance: Require customs and terminal operators to feed real-time duty/fuel and vessel data; audit platform fees for small traders; reserve lanes/tolls for small vehicles during peak seasons. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Coupling ERP/TMS with predictive analytics uses real-time customs, port, and transport data to model disruptions and adjust flows</cite>.
- Complementary supply: Incentivize local blending plants and galvanized iron substitutes; parallel track duty-free vs. duty-paid corridors with digital traceability to reduce smuggling-driven volatility. <cite id="c85950f1-0">Past large-scale cement capacity additions lowered prices materially</cite>.

Bottom line
- Evidence supports that AI-driven digital integration can materially reduce price volatility risk in construction material supply chains by improving early warning, forecasts, procurement, and logistics continuity; quantitative studies show meaningful forecast accuracy gains and feasibility of real-time budgeting under high inflation and disruption. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-0">Predictive analytics provides actionable forecasts and disruption early warnings for steel, concrete, lumber, enabling early procurement or delay</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Predictive analytics improves accuracy by 20–50%, reduces inventory volatility, and moderates crisis-period price increases by maintaining supply continuity</cite> <cite id="da55d358-0">ARIMA/multiple regression achieved 1.4–2.8% MAPE for key materials in Egypt, enabling tighter budgeting</cite> <cite id="da55d358-2">Automated, data-integrated cost workflows adjusted budgets monthly during 101% cement and 134% steel increases</cite>.
- Evidence from Ethiopia/Addis Ababa shows that structural factors—informality, shortages, regulation, and land speculation—keep volatility high; digitalization layered on top of these can reduce, but not eliminate, swings without broader infrastructure, market-structure, and policy reforms. <cite id="c85950f1-3">Chronic shortages of corrugated iron and concrete slabs and tight financing/equipment access in Addis Ababa contribute to delays and cost volatility</cite> <cite id="193dc8e6-4">Three-quarters of land in major Ethiopian cities is supplied informally, sustaining high and speculative prices that transmit into construction costs</cite> <cite id="c85950f1-0">Cement prices fell after large-capacity entry, demonstrating supply capacity’s stabilizing role</cite>.

Conclusion
- Can AI-driven digital integration “eliminate” volatility? Unlikely alone. It can reliably reduce volatility by cutting information and coordination frictions and by enabling proactive procurement and logistics; documented accuracy gains and case implementations show strong risk mitigation. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-0">Forecast-driven decisions and early warnings mitigate variance</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Improved responsiveness moderates price increases and reduces inventory volatility</cite> <cite id="da55d358-0">Low-MAPE forecasting supports tighter budgeting</cite>.
- To approach near-term volatility reduction in Addis Ababa’s informal markets, combine platformization with infrastructure upgrades, open data mandates, anti-monopoly oversight, and complementary local capacity; success will be measurable by lower price dispersion and shorter lead times for key inputs, with residual volatility tied to global macro and speculative real estate cycles. <cite id="da55d358-4">Real-time API and blockchain-enhanced data sharing reduces regional disparities and fraud</cite> <cite id="193dc8e6-4">Informal land/speculative markets are a core structural driver that digitalization alone cannot remove</cite>.

Title: Impact of Inflation on Construction Cost Estimation: Strategies to Account for Fluctuating Material Prices
Snippet: AI driven predictive analytics has become a fast emerging means of dealing with the impact of inflation on construction cost estimation. Accuracy in material price trend forecast is invaluable given the level of cost volatility in an industry where project timelines and profitability are subject to significant impacts. For example by analyzing patterns in the pricing of key materials like steel, concrete, and lumber, predictive models can forecast price movements to help contractors decide whether to procure materials early in anticipation of price hikes, or delay purchases if price drop is anticipated [12]. Predictive analytics tools can provide not just forecasts of material prices but of other trends in the supply chain, such as potential vulnerabilities. These tools continuously monitor supply chain performance to pick up early warning signals for disruptions, like delays in shipping, factory shut downs or geopolitical unrest that could result in rising prices, or shortages in crucial raw materials. For example, when predictive analytics reflect a slowdown in the manufacture of cement because of a labor strike that disrupts a key production plant, contractors may take proactive steps, like securing alternative suppliers or purchasing materials in advance, neither of which would be desirable under the short-term inflation spike driven inflationary surge in material prices [13]. 

In a post pandemic world where the supply chain has become more unpredictable and disrupted these capabilities are even more important. This isn't just about increasing the accuracy of cost estimates, it's also about improving how we manage risk and plan projects. The inclusion of predictive tools in the processes for constructing a budget can allow construction firms to foresee inflationary pressure that will impact project timelines before the effects are realized and correct accordingly to mitigate the fallout from greater variance, thereby enhancing financial performance. Title: Optimizing construction supply chains through AI: Streamlining material procurement and logistics for project success
Snippet: The construction industry faces numerous challenges in achieving efficient supply chains, particularly in material procurement and logistics. This paper explores the transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in addressing these challenges and enhancing project success. The discussion covers current issues in construction supply chains, the pivotal role of AI in revolutionizing material procurement and logistics, and practical strategies for implementation. The paper delves into the fragmented communication, inefficient procurement processes, and limited logistics visibility that hinder construction supply chains. AI's application is examined in real-time data analytics, automation of procurement workflows, and the integration of intelligent logistics management systems. The implementation of AI in material procurement includes demand forecasting, automated vendor selection, and order tracking, while logistics streamlining encompasses real-time tracking, route optimization, and proactive delay management. Benefits of AI implementation are highlighted, including cost reduction through waste minimization and optimized logistics, increased efficiency in procurement processes, and improved project timelines. The paper incorporates case studies illustrating successful AI implementation in construction supply chains, showcasing tangible improvements in material procurement and logistics. Despite the evident benefits, the paper acknowledges challenges and considerations in AI adoption within the construction industry. Barriers to implementation are discussed, along with strategies to overcome resistance and ensure successful integration. By streamlining material procurement and logistics through AI, construction projects can achieve heightened efficiency, reduced costs, and improved collaboration among stakeholders, ultimately contributing to overall project success.

Title: Construction Material Market Volatility on Project Budgetary Risk and Contingency Planning
Snippet: There has been a rise in consideration of material cost fluctuations as a critical challenge to the construction industry especially to civil projects where material costs represent a considerable percentage of the total budget. Not only they cause budget overruns, but these fluctuations also cause project delays, contractual disputes, and have therefore acute need for efficient risk mitigation strategies.

The case studies examined show in how construction projects in different regions have reacted to the consequences of material cost volatility by using different strategies to varying degrees of success. The global economy's volatility continues and now it's more important than ever for construction companies to be able to be agile and proactive with managing material costs. Such monitoring of market trends includes strong supplier relationships and investing in training and development programs for developing teams with the adaptability for changes in conditions. Title: Information System-Based Predictive Analytics to Reduce Supply Chain Disruptions and Inflation in the United States
Snippet: Advanced enterprise resource planning (ERP), warehouse management systems (WMS), and transportation management systems (TMS) support multidirectional information flows that are essential for harmonizing demand and supply signals. When coupled with predictive analytics, machine learning, and artificial intelligence (AI), these systems provide probabilistic forecasts that allow firms to anticipate demand surges, detect early signals of supplier distress, and model how disruptions propagate across network nodes. Research indicates that predictive analytics improve forecasting accuracy by 20-50%, reduce inventory volatility, and lower operational risk exposure [4]. In macroeconomic terms, improved forecasting strengthens price stability by reducing stockouts, lowering procurement premiums, and preventing panic-driven supply chain reactions that historically accelerate inflation [5]. Predictive analytics in supply chain applications employ a wide range of methods, including supervised learning, anomaly detection, deep learning architectures, graph-based modeling of network interdependencies, and econometric forecasting of inflationary pass-through. These methods operate on high-velocity data generated from sensors, RFID systems, GPS telemetry, customs records, e-commerce transactions, port activity logs, and financial indicators. Integrating these data streams through information systems creates a unified analytical environment where machine-learning models can detect complex, nonlinear patterns that traditional forecasting models often fail to capture. For instance, AI-driven models have demonstrated superior accuracy in predicting transportation delays and demand spikes during extreme weather events or geopolitical shocks [6]. In the context of inflation mitigation, predictive analytics contributes by stabilizing supply-demand imbalances that often lead to price escalation. When disruptions are detected early, firms can initiate alternative sourcing, adjust safety-stock thresholds, diversify transportation routes, and coordinate with federal or regional authorities to pre-empt shortages. Empirical research confirms that improved logistical responsiveness moderates price increases during crisis periods by maintaining supply continuity and preventing panic buying [7]. Moreover, digital twins-virtual replicas of supply chain networks-allow scenario-based simulations that identify optimal decision paths to minimize cost escalations and service interruptions [8].
</snippet>

Around 2000, the United Nations' Millennial Development Goals called for action to address issues of environmental sustainability and poverty reduction [13]. Recent surveys estimate that percent of people living in poverty is continuing to decline. In 2015/16, the Ethiopian government reported that 23.5% of its population lived beneath the poverty line and this figure was 16.8% in Addis Ababa. Despite these gains, Ethiopia is still a relatively poor country (ranked 164/187 by the World Bank in 2017) but it aspires to become a lower middle-income nation by 2025 [15].

Title: Urban land management under rapid urbanization: Exploring the link between urban land policies and urban land use efficiency in Ethiopia
Snippet: The combination of these factors has pushed people to engage in the informal land transfer market, primarily in urban peripheries. This has resulted in extensive urban sprawl, land use fragmentation, and the proliferation of informal settlements across major Ethiopian cities (MoUDHC & ECSU, 2015;World Bank, 2015). Similar challenges are faced by several African cities, where the failure of formal land markets forces urban dwellers into informal land markets (Home, 2021;UN-Habitat, 2010a), contributing to rampant urban sprawl (Li, 2020;Mboup & Oyelaran-Oyeyinka, 2019). 

The inefficiency of the formal land market has several adverse impacts on urban land utilization. Firstly, the government's inability to provide serviced land at affordable prices leads to high land prices and encourages corruption. Distortions in the land market contribute to extensive urban sprawl, as powerful individuals and companies acquire land without concrete plans for development, using it mainly for speculative purposes (ENA, 2018;Mengistu & van Dijk, 2018;Li Zhang & Xu, 2016). This acquisition of land for speculative purposes is widespread in Ethiopia and contributes to land hoarding, vacancy, and the hindrance of densification efforts (Mohamed et al., 2020;Payne & Durand-Lasserve, 2012). Deliberate scarcity of land supply in the formal sector serves vested interests, such as politically connected developers and corrupt officials (UN-Habitat, 2010a). The exceptionally high land prices in Ethiopia, disproportionate to the population's income and the country's economic situation, may be the result of market manipulation by vested interests. The scarcity of land supply in the formal sector has led to residential land being almost exclusively served by the informal sector (Lamson-Hall et al., 2019;World Bank Group, 2019). 

The formal land market's inefficiency has also contributed to widespread land speculation in Ethiopia, particularly in Addis Ababa and surrounding cities (Mohamed et al., 2020). About 75 % of the land is supplied via informal market either by speculators or farmers in periurban areas (Fransen & van Dijk, 2008).

Title: Addis Ababa Urbanism: Indigenous Urban Legacies and Contemporary Challenges
Snippet: One of the most striking features of the Addis Ababa cityscape today is the extent of buildings under construction. The first impression is of a construction boom that suggests a positive dynamic momentum. At a closer look, however, many of these construction sites are half-finished office and apartment buildings that do not exhibit any signs of construction activity (Fig. 5). The Ethiopian government not only owns all land that is leased to private enterprises for a ninety-nine-year period; it also regulates prices of construction materials and company permits, access to financing and construction equipment. Private sector lending is restricted to short term loans with high annual interest rates while initial investment is required to comprise at least thirty-five percent of the estimated project's cost (Tesfahunegn, 1999). These strict regulations have been the main reason for the bulk of unfinished and often abandoned construction sites in Addis Ababa that create a peculiar impression of the city being in a permanent state of construction in progress. The chronic deficit of the most commonly used construction materials such as corrugated iron sheets and reinforced concrete slabs is an additional factor that determines delays in construction. The only construction material that seems to be in good supply is eucalyptus round wood used for scaffolding as well as for checa in low quality residential structures. 

The demand for the eucalyptus wood material supports one of the most common types of informal activities in the city usually carried out by women who can be seen hauling enormous piles of eucalyptus poles on their backs from the surrounding woods. 

Due to the abundance of unfinished construction sites, the city air is polluted with suspended construction cement that poses a tangible health hazard, especially during dry winter months. Cement dust is mixed with unrestricted car exhaust, the second hazardous component of the city's air pollution due to the lack of exhaust regulations and the prevalence of used outdated automobiles in the streets. Most taxi cabs in Addis Ababa, popularly termed the "blue taxis", are old models of Lada, low quality automobiles that were built in the Soviet Union in cooperation with the Italian Fiat in the city of Tolyatti on the Volga River. Until recently, the city's public transportation demand was satisfied by the obsolete models of minivans, mostly former Soviet RAF once manufactured in Latvia, or VW minivans, in equally bad shape.
</snippet>

Title: Prediction of construction material prices using ARIMA and multiple regression models
Snippet: Construction material prices (CMP) variations have become a major issue in properly budgeting construction projects. Inability to accurately forecast CMP volatility can also lead to price overestimation or underestimation. Enhancing the accuracy of predictions of CMP can also enhance the accuracy of predictions of total construction costs. The purpose of this study is to present a model for predicting construction material prices that assist decision-makers to make better decisions over the life cycle of a project. The price records for CMP namely; steel, cement, brick, ceramic, and gravel, and the indicators affecting them in Egypt were used for the prediction procedures. The practical methods for using the Box-Jenkins approach Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) time series and multiple regression models for forecasting building material prices are outlined in this research. Out-of-sample predictions are used to evaluate the provided model’s performance in predicting future prices. The models are compared according to the Mean Absolute Percentage Errors (MAPE). The generated models show good results in predicting month-to-month variations in material prices, with MAPE ranging from 1.4 to 2.8 percent for the selected models. This research can assist both owners and contractors in improving their budgeting processes, and preparing more accurate cost estimates.
</snippet>

Title: The Impact of Material Price Fluctuation on Cost Overruns in National Toll Road Infrastructure Projects
Snippet: Fluctuations in construction material prices significantly challenge infrastructure project management, especially in Indonesia’s national toll road sector from 2023 to 2025. Employing a quantitative approach with purposive sampling of National Strategic Toll Road Projects (PSN), this study investigates the impact of price volatility for core materials (cement, steel, and asphalt) on project cost overruns. The analysis utilizes dual-source data: secondary data from the official Wholesale Price Index (WPI) published by the Central Statistics Agency (BPS) and budget realization data from the Ministry of Public Works and Housing (PUPR)/BPJT. Advanced analytical methods, including Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) to establish causal relationships and Least Squares Support Vector Machine (LSSVM) to develop a predictive model, reveal strong positive correlations between material price fluctuations and cost increases, with steel price volatility having the most pronounced effect. Empirical findings show cement prices increased by approximately 12.5% and steel by 15.3%, leading to cost overruns contributing up to 21% additional project costs. High reliability (Cronbach’s alpha 0.89) and data validity support these findings. Practical implications include the need for real-time price monitoring, adaptive budgeting with contingency funds of 20–25%, flexible procurement contracts, and digital tools like Building Information Modeling for risk mitigation. This research bridges macroeconomic volatility and engineering practice by offering an actionable predictive framework to support fiscal integrity and timely project delivery. Further research should incorporate socio-political variables and enhance predictive analytics using big data.
</snippet>

Title: BIM integration for cost management included inflation and market volatility
Snippet: A real case study involves 316 identical residential buildings across seven governorates, comprising more than 25,000 units. The construction of these buildings began in 2021 and concluded in 2024. During this period, there were significant global economic changes, including supply chain disruptions and rising inflation rates. These factors had a notable impact on the prices of raw materials, particularly steel and cement. Price data for these materials were obtained from CAPMAS, which publishes an annual bulletin of industrial material and product prices that serves as a reference for government economic indicators. The most notable result was as follows: 

From 2021 to 2023, steel and cement prices exhibited significant increases, with steel prices rising by 134.36% and cement prices increasing by 101.25%. This analysis was conducted using the percentage increase formula: The average steel price per ton in 2021 was approximately 14,971.02 EGP, which surged to 35,088.21 EGP in 2023, more than doubling over the period. Similarly, cement prices rose from an average of 965.2 EGP per ton in 2021 to 1,941.4 EGP per ton in 2023, marking a 101.25% increase. While both materials experienced substantial price hikes, steel prices exhibited greater volatility, as shown in Fig. 3. The significant increases in steel (134.36%) and cement (101.25%) prices observed in the study are consistent with broader economic trends documented by the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS). According to the Egypt Construction Market Report -Q4 2023 [17], construction material inflation in Egypt was primarily driven by currency devaluation, global supply chain disruptions, and rising energy costs. These economic conditions directly influenced the cost of key construction inputs, reinforcing the validity of the observed price surges. The proposed framework was practically applied in a residential construction project conducted between 2022 and 2023. It incorporated monthly CAPMAS bulletins and industry market reports into the automated cost estimation workflow. This integration enabled the framework to perform real-time budget adjustments in response to market dynamics, thereby demonstrating its operational feasibility and adaptability to economic volatility.
</snippet>

Snippet: The construction market in Hudur, which is impacted by volatility in the prices of building materials such as cement and galvanized iron sheets, presents significant challenges for a city's infrastructure development and economic growth. The fluctuating prices, driven by factors such as demand shifts, raw material costs, and market dynamics, affect the affordability and feasibility of construction projects. The peak in cement prices in 2015, followed by a gradual decline and subsequent increase in 2021, illustrates the market's sensitivity to economic conditions and technological advancements (see Table 6). This volatility not only raises the cost of construction but also impacts broader housing and infrastructure development, making it difficult for stakeholders to plan and budget effectively. To mitigate the risks associated with price volatility in the construction market, Hudur needs to adopt a climate-responsive approach that emphasizes sustainable building practices and materials.

Title: Building material price data for predictive cost estimation in construction
Snippet: This study introduces the Building Materials Dataset as a comprehensive resource for analyzing historical and real-time fluctuations in construction material prices in Nigeria. The dataset was compiled through structured surveys with material suppliers and secondary data from reputable online marketplaces and industry reports. Designed to support cost estimation, procurement planning, and financial forecasting, it enables researchers, policymakers, and industry professionals to assess market trends, optimize budgeting strategies, and mitigate financial risks associated with price volatility. Structured in a tabular, time-series format, the dataset captures key information on material types, pricing variations over multiple years, and economic factors influencing costs. Preprocessing steps included data cleaning, Min-Max normalization, and feature engineering to enhance predictive modeling. The dataset was integrated into the BuildCES system, where a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model was applied for price prediction and cost estimation, facilitating data-driven procurement optimization and contract management. Future enhancements will incorporate Blockchain technology to ensure transaction transparency, real-time pricing updates via API integration, and geospatial data mapping to analyze regional price disparities. By systematically documenting construction material prices in Nigeria, this dataset addresses the gap in structured data availability, providing a scalable foundation for research, industry benchmarking, and policy development. By fostering a data-driven approach to construction management, the dataset contributes to economic stability, transparency, and sustainability in the industry.

Summary answer
- Short answer: AI-driven digital integration of construction material supply chains can substantially reduce, but not reliably eliminate, price volatility in Addis Ababa’s informal markets. Mechanism-based and empirical studies show that integrated data, predictive analytics, and connected logistics enable earlier warning of disruptions, more accurate demand/supply forecasts, and proactive procurement and routing that moderate spikes and shortages. In Ethiopia and similar LMIC contexts, digitized price data and platform integrations have improved forecasting accuracy and supported adaptive contracting and procurement; however, structural features of Addis Ababa’s markets—deep informality, shortages of key items, and regulatory frictions—mean platform-only solutions are unlikely to fully stabilize prices without complementary reforms and infrastructure. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-0">AI-driven predictive analytics can forecast movements in key construction materials (steel, concrete, lumber) and warn of disruptions (e.g., factory shutdowns, shipping slowdowns), enabling early procurement or delay decisions that directly mitigate volatility exposure</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-1">AI-enabled procurement and logistics (demand forecasting, automated vendor selection, real-time tracking, route optimization) cut waste, reduce costs, and improve continuity, which dampen volatility-driven overruns</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Predictive analytics improves forecast accuracy by 20–50%, reduces inventory volatility, and moderates price spikes by preventing panic reactions and enabling alternative sourcing and safety-stock adjustments</cite> <cite id="da55d358-0">Time-series models (ARIMA, multiple regression) for construction material prices in Egypt achieved 1.4–2.8% MAPE, demonstrating that accurate forecasting is feasible to support better budgeting under price swings</cite> <cite id="da55d358-4">A Nigeria dataset integrating supplier surveys and online marketplace data feeds into LSTM price prediction and procurement optimization, with proposed API and blockchain integrations for real-time pricing and transparency to address regional price disparities</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-4">AI-driven analytics help identify market trends early, minimizing financial impact of short-term volatility via early procurement, bulk buying, and escalation clauses</cite>.

- Evidence in Ethiopia/Addis Ababa: The city’s construction ecosystem is shaped by informality, regulation, and chronic shortages (e.g., corrugated iron, concrete slabs), which heighten sensitivity to logistics and policy shocks; yet large-scale investments (e.g., Dangote cement) have pushed cement prices down from >500 to <250 birr, indicating that supply-side capacity expansion can meaningfully dampen price levels and swings. However, informality and land speculation dominate land and housing markets, implying persistent frictions that can transmit shocks to material markets. <cite id="c85950f1-0">Ethiopia’s cement sector saw prices fall from 500 birr+ to under 250 birr after Dangote’s large plant, illustrating supply expansion’s stabilizing effect on prices</cite> <cite id="c85950f1-3">Addis Ababa exhibits many half-finished buildings and chronic shortages of common materials (corrugated iron, reinforced concrete slabs), with tight regulations and a shortage of construction equipment and financing contributing to delays and cost volatility</cite> <cite id="c85950f1-3">The government regulates material prices and construction equipment access, reinforcing that policy and logistics constraints, not only market forces, drive volatility</cite> <cite id="193dc8e6-4">In Ethiopia, about three-quarters of urban land supply in major cities flows through informal markets due to formal market inefficiencies and speculation, which contributes to high and unstable land and construction costs</cite>.

- What refutes “eliminate”: Multiple studies and Addis Ababa’s institutional context show that volatility stems from macro shocks, geopolitics, energy/fuel costs, supply chain disruptions, and structural informality/speculation; digital integration reduces exposure but cannot remove these structural drivers absent broader reforms. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-2">Supply chain disruptions, geopolitical instability, and inflation are primary drivers of material price volatility, causing overruns, delays, and disputes, necessitating proactive risk mitigation</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-0">Early warning of shipping delays, factory shutdowns, and geopolitical unrest via AI enables mitigation, but such shocks are external and recurrent</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Improved forecasting reduces panic-driven reactions and stockouts, but volatility persists when disruptions propagate across networks</cite> <cite id="193dc8e6-0">Ethiopian urban grain market studies find no clear difference in volatility across markets, with trends rising—suggesting persistence even when information flows integrate</cite> <cite id="193dc8e6-4">Informal land/speculative markets keep supply tight and prices elevated, making volatility hard to eradicate by ICT alone</cite>.

Mechanisms by which digital/AI integration can reduce volatility
- Early warning and disruption analytics: AI over ERP/WMS/TMS data (customs, sensors, GPS, e-commerce) detects supplier distress, transport delays, and geopolitical shocks that propagate into material price spikes, enabling rerouting, alternative sourcing, and inventory adjustments. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-0">Monitoring for strikes, shipping slowdowns, and factory shutdowns lets contractors procure alternatives or adjust timing to avoid spikes</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Predictive systems with ML detect demand surges and transport delays (e.g., extreme weather, geopolitics), allowing pre-emptive rerouting and sourcing that prevent panic buying and stabilize prices</cite>.
- Demand/supply forecasting and procurement optimization: Machine learning on historical and real-time data improves forecast accuracy, supports dynamic purchasing windows, and integrates with BIM and ERP for rolling budget updates. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-1">Demand forecasting, automated vendor selection, and order tracking reduce procurement cycle waste and costs</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-4">AI-driven analytics spot market trends early so early procurement or flexible escalation clauses minimize financial impact of short-term surges</cite> <cite id="da55d358-0">ARIMA and regression models achieved 1.4–2.8% MAPE for steel, cement, brick, ceramic, gravel in Egypt, enabling tighter budgeting under volatility</cite> <cite id="da55d358-2">Integrating monthly price bulletins into automated cost workflows enabled real-time budget adjustments during 101% cement and 134% steel increases (2021–2023), showing feasibility of adaptive frameworks</cite>.
- Logistics continuity and inventory smoothing: Real-time tracking, route optimization, and digital twins simulate disruptions and adjust safety stocks, reducing service interruptions and procurement premiums. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-1">Real-time logistics visibility and proactive delay management streamline flows and reduce costs</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">AI forecasting improves by 20–50%, lowers inventory volatility, and predictive models cut procurement premiums by maintaining continuity and preventing panic-driven price hikes</cite>.
- Data ecosystems and transparency: Aggregating supplier reports, marketplace prices, and macro indicators into unified platforms improves price discovery and reduces regional disparities; proposed Blockchain/APIs further ensure timely updates and auditability. <cite id="da55d358-4">A Nigeria dataset compiles supplier and online marketplace prices, integrates them into LSTM forecasting within a procurement system (BuildCES), and proposes API and blockchain to deliver real-time, transparent pricing and reduce regional disparities</cite>.

Evidence from Ethiopia and Addis Ababa: feasibility and limits
- Ethiopia’s cement example shows large swings can be countered by supply-side capacity and data-driven procurement strategies. <cite id="c85950f1-0">After Dangote’s plant, cement prices fell from 500+ to under 250 birr, directly cutting a major input’s volatility footprint and benefiting housing projects</cite>. This suggests digital integration layered on top of expanded capacity can stabilize prices more broadly.
- However, Addis Ababa’s regulatory environment and shortages create frictions that transmit shocks. <cite id="c85950f1-3">Shortages of corrugated iron and reinforced concrete slabs and high costs of capital equipment cause delays and cost volatility</cite> <cite id="c85950f1-3">Price and equipment regulation, short-term high-interest lending, and large share of owner-finance lead to underbuilding and sensitivity to input shocks</cite>. Informality and speculation in land/real estate mean housing and materials demand remain volatile. <cite id="193dc8e6-4">About 75% of land in major Ethiopian cities is supplied via informal channels—driven by formal market failures—contributing to high and speculative land prices that ripple into construction costs</cite>.
- Evidence from Addis Ababa’s construction sites shows that despite appearances of a boom, chronic material deficits persist, indicating structural supply and logistics issues beyond what ICT can fix alone. <cite id="c85950f1-3">Many half-finished buildings and persistent shortages point to supply-chain and logistics bottlenecks, not only demand-side volatility</cite>.

Evidence from LMIC construction markets on digital mitigation of volatility
- Forecasting precision and decision support: <cite id="da55d358-0">Egypt models achieved 1.4–2.8% MAPE for five key materials, supporting better budgeting and reducing over/underestimation errors</cite> <cite id="da55d358-2">A seven-governorate residential build-inventory case integrated monthly price bulletins into cost workflows to perform real-time budget adjustments amid 101% cement and 134% steel increases (2021–2023)</cite>. - Data-driven procurement platforms: <cite id="da55d358-4">Nigeria’s Building Materials Dataset integrates supplier surveys and online marketplace data, feeds an LSTM-based estimator in BuildCES, and proposes API and blockchain for real-time price updates and transparency to address regional price disparities</cite>. - Macro-infrastructure linkages: <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Digital integration of customs, logistics, and market data reduces stockouts and procurement premiums, moderating crisis-period price increases</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-1">Automated workflows and real-time tracking reduce waste and improve efficiency, lowering cost variance exposure</cite>.
- Quantified sensitivity: <cite id="da55d358-1">In Indonesia’s toll roads (2023–2025), empirical modeling found strong positive correlations between cement, steel, and asphalt price volatility and cost overruns (steel had the largest effect), with cement up ~12.5% and steel ~15.3%, contributing up to 21% additional project costs; recommended responses include real-time price monitoring and digital tools like BIM</cite>. This reinforces that digital monitoring and analytics are key mitigants, but not panaceas.

Evidence that can refute over-optimism
- Structural volatility sources: <cite id="7ee6d9c7-2">Supply chain disruptions, geopolitical instability, and inflation remain principal drivers of material price volatility, causing overruns and disputes</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-0">AI can only anticipate some shocks (e.g., factory shutdowns, shipping slowdowns); unpredictable geopolitical events can overwhelm localized analytics</cite>.
- Market power and platformization: While not Ethiopia-specific, digitalization can create new concentration risks (e.g., dominant platforms, data monopolies) that suppress competition and sustain price dispersion; absent antitrust and open-data mandates, digital integration may not lower prices for informal actors. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-1">Fragmented communication and limited visibility are core frictions; integration depends on stakeholder collaboration and data sharing, which can be blocked by incumbents</cite>.
- Infrastructure constraints: Digital gains require reliable energy, connectivity, and trusted data flows; in Ethiopian urban peripheries, logistics and payment frictions persist. <cite id="c85950f1-3">Shortages and equipment constraints slow delivery even when orders are placed</cite> <cite id="da55d358-4">Regional price disparities persist, motivating API-driven real-time updates and transparency to correct asymmetries</cite>.
- Informality and speculation: <cite id="193dc8e6-4">Three-quarters of land supply in major Ethiopian cities flows through informal channels, with speculation and hoarding inflating prices and making markets brittle to information shocks</cite>. Digital platforms may not reach unbanked, small traders without mobile money and regulatory support.

What would further support or refute the claim
- Field experiments in Addis Ababa: A randomized rollout of an integrated platform for cement, sand, and bricks linking mini-markets, wholesalers, and transporters with real-time price feeds, predictive alerts, and mobile money payments, measuring changes in price dispersion and short-run volatility versus control sites. <cite id="da55d358-4">API-integrated real-time price updates and blockchain-audited transactions are proposed to reduce disparities and fraud</cite>.
- Quasi-experimental expansion of state or port/customs digitization in Ethiopia: Measuring post-digitization reductions in delivery times and price premiums for construction inputs, controlling for macro shocks. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Improved responsiveness moderates price increases during crises by maintaining supply continuity</cite>.
- Inclusion mandates: Studies assessing effects of open data portals or mandated API sharing with small suppliers on price stability and trader revenues. <cite id="da55d358-4">Open, integrated data ecosystems reduce regional price disparities and enable procurement optimization</cite>.

Practical pathway for Addis Ababa
- Anchor with infrastructure: Expand metered electricity and LTE/5G coverage to mini-markets and transport nodes; pair with affordable mobile data plans for traders. <cite id="da55d358-4">Real-time APIs and geospatial mapping are needed to correct regional disparities</cite>.
- Build an Addis Ababa Construction Materials Data Commons: Aggregate daily prices from 50+ traders/wholesalers via structured SMS/API, integrate port/customs/duty and fuel indices, and publish open dashboards. <cite id="da55d358-4">A structured time-series dataset of suppliers and online marketplaces enables forecasting and procurement optimization</cite>.
- Platform features: 
  - Predictive early-warning panel (steel, cement, sand, bricks) with procurement recommendations and vendor network routing. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-0">Forecasting and disruption warnings guide early buy vs. delay decisions</cite>.
  - Dynamic escalation/contingency clauses and rolling budgets tied to market indices, implemented in BIM/ERP. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-4">Escalation clauses and early trend detection reduce financial impact</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-1">ERP-BIM integration supports rolling cost updates</cite>.
  - Logistics optimization and vehicle routing with real-time rerouting for duty-free corridors. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-1">Route optimization and proactive delay management reduce costs</cite>.
- Governance: Require customs and terminal operators to feed real-time duty/fuel and vessel data; audit platform fees for small traders; reserve lanes/tolls for small vehicles during peak seasons. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Coupling ERP/TMS with predictive analytics uses real-time customs, port, and transport data to model disruptions and adjust flows</cite>.
- Complementary supply: Incentivize local blending plants and galvanized iron substitutes; parallel track duty-free vs. duty-paid corridors with digital traceability to reduce smuggling-driven volatility. <cite id="c85950f1-0">Past large-scale cement capacity additions lowered prices materially</cite>.

Bottom line
- Evidence supports that AI-driven digital integration can materially reduce price volatility risk in construction material supply chains by improving early warning, forecasts, procurement, and logistics continuity; quantitative studies show meaningful forecast accuracy gains and feasibility of real-time budgeting under high inflation and disruption. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-0">Predictive analytics provides actionable forecasts and disruption early warnings for steel, concrete, lumber, enabling early procurement or delay</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Predictive analytics improves accuracy by 20–50%, reduces inventory volatility, and moderates crisis-period price increases by maintaining supply continuity</cite> <cite id="da55d358-0">ARIMA/multiple regression achieved 1.4–2.8% MAPE for key materials in Egypt, enabling tighter budgeting</cite> <cite id="da55d358-2">Automated, data-integrated cost workflows adjusted budgets monthly during 101% cement and 134% steel increases</cite>.
- Evidence from Ethiopia/Addis Ababa shows that structural factors—informality, shortages, regulation, and land speculation—keep volatility high; digitalization layered on top of these can reduce, but not eliminate, swings without broader infrastructure, market-structure, and policy reforms. <cite id="c85950f1-3">Chronic shortages of corrugated iron and concrete slabs and tight financing/equipment access in Addis Ababa contribute to delays and cost volatility</cite> <cite id="193dc8e6-4">Three-quarters of land in major Ethiopian cities is supplied informally, sustaining high and speculative prices that transmit into construction costs</cite> <cite id="c85950f1-0">Cement prices fell after large-capacity entry, demonstrating supply capacity’s stabilizing role</cite>.

Conclusion
- Can AI-driven digital integration “eliminate” volatility? Unlikely alone. It can reliably reduce volatility by cutting information and coordination frictions and by enabling proactive procurement and logistics; documented accuracy gains and case implementations show strong risk mitigation. <cite id="7ee6d9c7-0">Forecast-driven decisions and early warnings mitigate variance</cite> <cite id="7ee6d9c7-3">Improved responsiveness moderates price increases and reduces inventory volatility</cite> <cite id="da55d358-0">Low-MAPE forecasting supports tighter budgeting</cite>.
- To approach near-term volatility reduction in Addis Ababa’s informal markets, combine platformization with infrastructure upgrades, open data mandates, anti-monopoly oversight, and complementary local capacity; success will be measurable by lower price dispersion and shorter lead times for key inputs, with residual volatility tied to global macro and speculative real estate cycles. <cite id="da55d358-4">Real-time API and blockchain-enhanced data sharing reduces regional disparities and fraud</cite> <cite id="193dc8e6-4">Informal land/speculative markets are a core structural driver that digitalization alone cannot remove</cite>.
</answer>
