- Digital product/material passports and cataloging: Each building/stockpile should reference material passports or supplier catalogs to capture type, quantity, quality, and reuse instructions. <cite id="ed23621d-0">DPP–BIM integration improves traceability and reuse but is hampered by interoperability, governance, and procurement integration gaps</cite>. <cite id="ed23621d-1">Where materials lack GTINs (custom or individual pieces), material passports can fill gaps and be combined with a digital construction logistics twin; keeping such data current is a major challenge, and data entry capacity often resides with executing companies</cite>.
- Standards and identifiers (GS1/GTIN, catalog schemas): Standardized identifiers and catalog schemas reduce ambiguity for heterogeneous construction materials. <cite id="ed23621d-1">The presented digital construction logistics twin approach does not cover items without GTINs (e.g., tools, formwork, scaffolding), motivating the use of material passports and highlighting the need to reduce manual entry and agreed update workflows</cite>.

3) Supply-chain sensing, tracking, and provenance
- ERP/WMS/procurement integration: Systems that record orders, receipts, storage locations, and issuance must interoperate with BIM/GIS so AI can map materials from origin to site/stockpile to building. <cite id="ed23621d-0">Fragmented supply chains, unclear data governance, and limited integration with procurement systems are persistent barriers to DPP–BIM deployment</cite>. <cite id="4c662045-0">AI can optimize procurement and logistics by unifying fragmented communication, automating vendor selection and order tracking, and integrating intelligent logistics management with real‑time tracking and route optimization</cite>.
- Transport and material tracking (IoT/RFID/telematics): Real‑time or near‑real‑time movement data ensure the “ground truth” for material flows that AI models will predict and monitor. <cite id="ed23621d-2">Transport and material tracking systems digitally trace materials; material passports store type/quantity/location/recycling instructions; blockchain provides immutable provenance and smart contracts; IoT sensors/RFID enable real‑time inventory and logistics coordination</cite>.
- Enforcement and sharing protocols: City logistics intelligence requires cross‑stakeholder data access and governance. <cite id="4c662045-2">City planners can track urban freight flows and adjust policy via real‑time dashboards in smart‑city logistics frameworks</cite>. <cite id="ed23621d-1">It will be important to check whether executing companies are willing to share logistics data and add it to BIM; many SMEs lack expertise, software, and personnel, suggesting delegation of data entry/management to a participant and agreement on regular updates</cite>.

4) AI/data/AI4I readiness for material mapping
- Sensor strategy and reference datasets: High‑quality imagery/scans (UAV/terrestrial, close‑range photogrammetry/LiDAR) plus labeled material catalogs to train and validate models. <cite id="c00d2579-0">There is a need for large, comprehensive construction‑specific image datasets; standards for collecting and protecting worker data; and application of object detection/tracking and 3D reconstruction to support on‑site tasks</cite>. <cite id="c00d2579-1">Common construction material categories like scaffolding couplers, footboards, steel tubes are often underrepresented in public datasets; custom datasets with augmentation (rain, snow, fog, motion blur) and 1,115 labeled annotations enabled few‑shot recognition for scaffolding assembly tasks</cite>. <cite id="c00d2579-2">Traditional numeric labels miss construction‑specific semantics; public datasets focus on common objects and lack essential tools/materials; manual labeling is time‑consuming; multimodal vision‑language learning can reduce samples and training time for construction tasks</cite>.
- Ontologies and taxonomies: Harmonized material/product taxonomies linked to BIM objects and supply‑chain records to resolve ambiguity across languages, brands, and local equivalents. <cite id="ed23621d-1">Standardization of exchange formats simplifies data fusion; many building components lack GTINs, necessitating material passports and workflows to keep data current</cite>.
- Cloud/AI platforms and pipelines: Secure, repeatable pipelines for data ingestion, labeling, model training/validation, deployment, and continuous learning with feedback from field scans and logs. <cite id="c00d2579-0">Emerging needs include standards for collecting and protecting personal data, and applying CV domains (pose estimation, 3D reconstruction) to support robotic applications</cite>.

5) Planning, industrial, and urban context integration
- Industrial planning and corridors: Align material mapping with industrial land use and transport networks to reflect where materials actually flow and where enforcement or incentives are needed. <cite id="4c662045-1">Industrialization has significant spatial impact; urban spatial planning should be flexible and coordinated with industrial strategy; planned urban growth corridors (e.g., Addis Ababa–Bishoftu) require close collaboration to manage investment flows, accessibility, and unplanned growth</cite>.
- Policy and capacity: Clear data governance, privacy, and interoperability policies, plus capacity building for SMEs and agencies. <cite id="ed23621d-0">Unified digital frameworks, policy development, and technological innovation are needed to overcome interoperability, governance, and procurement integration gaps for DPP–BIM</cite>. <cite id="ed23621d-1">Many SMEs lack expertise and tools to work with BIM; delegating data entry/management and agreeing on update cadence can keep a digital logistics twin current</cite>.

Recommended sequence (literature-backed staging)

Phase 0: Governance, standards, and data policies
- Establish city data governance for geospatial and logistics data; mandate harmonized identifiers (parcel/asset IDs, GTIN/GS1 where applicable) and define BIM/GIS integration requirements. <cite id="ed23621d-0">Interoperability gaps, unclear data governance, and limited procurement integration impede DPP–BIM adoption; unified frameworks and policy development are emphasized</cite>. <cite id="df5d2a0d-0">GIS frameworks can resolve data confusion when a city builds and uses a geodatabase for planning and service delivery</cite>.

Phase 1: Core city and building data foundations
- Populate and link a master geodatabase with GIS and BIM for all significant assets; ensure cadastral parcels and building footprints carry attributes (ownership, permits, codes). <cite id="df5d2a0d-0">Addis Ababa’s geodatabase built via GIS improved revenue collection, title issuance, and planning use</cite>. <cite id="ed23621d-2">GIS and BIM integrate spatial and building data to enable routing, reuse identification, and planning for circular logistics</cite>.
- Deploy material passports/digital product passports for new and major retrofit/build-out projects and link to BIM/GIS. <cite id="ed23621d-0">DPP–BIM integration improves traceability and reuse but requires overcoming interoperability and governance barriers</cite>. <cite id="ed23621d-1">Material passports cover components without GTINs and should be kept current via agreed update workflows</cite>.

Phase 2: Supply-chain and logistics sensing backbone
- Integrate ERP/WMS/procurement with BIM/GIS; instrument transport and stockpiles with RFID/IoT where feasible; install telematics for hauls; ensure material issuance/return records are digitalized. <cite id="ed23621d-0">Limited integration with procurement systems and fragmented supply chains are key barriers to material traceability</cite>. <cite id="ed23621d-2">Blockchain provides immutable provenance and smart contracts; IoT tracks components in real time to enable inventory management and logistics coordination</cite>. <cite id="4c662045-0">AI integration in procurement/logistics includes demand forecasting, automated vendor selection, real‑time tracking, and route optimization to reduce costs and waste</cite>.
- Stand up city logistics dashboards and digital-twin feedback loops for freight flows to calibrate AI predictions. <cite id="4c662045-2">Real‑time dashboards let planners track urban freight flows and adjust policy; AI‑driven route optimization and fleet monitoring improve supply chain efficiency</cite>.

Phase 3: AI/data pipelines for material mapping
- Deploy on‑site sensing (UAV/scan) and reference dataset curation for Addis Ababa’s material typology; build labeled catalogs from material passports/BIM and supplier catalogs; implement pipelines with continuous feedback from field scans and logistics data. <cite id="c00d2579-0">Large, comprehensive construction‑specific datasets and standards for data capture are needed; object detection/tracking and 3D reconstruction are the main CV domains in construction</cite>. <cite id="c00d2579-1">Few‑shot methods can work with small curated datasets augmented for adverse conditions; scaffolding materials central to Addis Ababa’s rapid construction are often underrepresented</cite>. <cite id="c00d2579-2">Multimodal vision‑language learning reduces samples and training time; public datasets miss essential construction tools/materials, underscoring the need for domain‑specific catalogs</cite>.
- Implement ontologies linking material IDs to BIM classes and supply‑chain records; enforce privacy and data protection. <cite id="c00d2579-0">Standards and practices for collecting and protecting personal data are needed alongside CV deployment</cite>. <cite id="ed23621d-1">Standardized exchange formats simplify fusion; GTIN gaps require material passports and clear update responsibilities</cite>.

Phase 4: Pilot and roll-out with circularity and enforcement goals
- Pilot AI mapping on a sub-city or corridor (e.g., Bole/Yeka/Kirkos) aligned with planned growth corridors; use outputs to target reuse, recycling, and compliance; feed results back into procurement and logistics optimization. <cite id="4c662045-1">Addis Ababa’s industrialization and urban growth corridors require coordinated planning; collaboration between Addis Ababa and adjacent cities (Galan, Dukem, Bishoftu) is essential to manage expansion and investment flows</cite>. <cite id="ed23621d-2">BIM acts as a living inventory to design for disassembly and streamline deconstruction; material passports and digital twins support proactive logistics planning and reuse</cite>. <cite id="4c662045-0">Case studies show AI implementation reduces costs via waste minimization and improves timelines through automated workflows and visibility</cite>.
- Iterate on governance and capacity: support SMEs and executing agencies with delegated data entry/management roles and regular update cadences. <cite id="ed23621d-1">SMEs often lack BIM expertise; delegating digital construction logistics twin management to a participant and agreeing on regular updates is critical</cite>.

Addis Ababa–specific adaptations and risks
- Informality and rapid industrialization: Industrialization has strong spatial effects; mapping must reflect where materials move and where planning enforcement is needed. <cite id="4c662045-1">Industrialization drives significant urban spatial outcomes; planning must align industrial locations and govern urbanization along corridors; collaboration between Addis Ababa and Bishoftu is needed to overcome unplanned growth and transport gaps</cite>.
- Data readiness and access: Logistics data sharing and update practices must be negotiated; build dashboards that planners can act on. <cite id="4c662045-2">AI logistics tools require managerial buy‑in and integration into operations to improve efficiency and inform policy</cite>. <cite id="ed23621d-1">Willingness of executing companies to share logistics data and add it to BIM is pivotal; standardization and delegated data stewardship help sustain an accurate digital logistics twin</cite>.
- Heterogeneous materials and local typologies: Many building components lack global GTINs; cataloging via material passports and local ontologies is essential. <cite id="ed23621d-1">Approaches that ignore items without GTINs miss critical components; material passports fill gaps but require sustained data updates</cite>. <cite id="c00d2579-1">Construction material categories like couplers and footboards are rarely collected/annotated; custom datasets with augmentation improved few‑shot recognition</cite>.

What to build first (practical checklist)
- Geospatial: master geodatabase tied to GIS and BIM for buildings; parcel/asset identifiers; GNSS/MMS protocols; QA/QC workflow for updates. <cite id="df5d2a0d-0">GIS geodatabases in Addis Ababa improved planning and revenue outcomes</cite>. <cite id="ed23621d-2">GIS/BIM integration supports routing, reuse identification, and planning</cite>.
- Catalog/provenance: supplier catalog ingestion (GTIN/GS1); local material passport creation for major stockpiles/buildings; link to BIM classes; privacy/bylaw data governance. <cite id="ed23621d-0">DPP–BIM integration must address interoperability, governance, and procurement linkage</cite>. <cite id="ed23621d-1">Material passports cover non‑GTIN items; standardization and update agreements are needed</cite>.
- Supply chain sensors: RFID/IoT on pallets/containers; telematics for hauls; ERP/WMS exports to BIM/GIS; agreed update cadence. <cite id="ed23621d-2">IoT/RFID track components; blockchain provides immutable provenance and smart contracts</cite>. <cite id="4c662045-0">AI procurement/logistics integration provides forecasting, automation, and route optimization</cite>.
- AI/data: UAV/scan fleet and QA; reference labeling lab tied to material passports; cloud ML pipelines; feedback loops from logistics dashboards; privacy-compliant data capture. <cite id="c00d2579-0">Construction CV benefits are real but depend on large, domain datasets and standards for data capture/protection</cite>. <cite id="c00d2579-1">Small curated, augmented datasets with precise labels enable few‑shot recognition for critical construction materials</cite>. <cite id="c00d2579-2">Multimodal vision‑language methods can reduce training data and time in complex construction scenes</cite>.
- Governance/capacity: data-sharing MOUs with suppliers/executives; SME support for data entry; pilot on a planned corridor; policy for updating twins; enforcement integration (inspect against mapped material records). <cite id="ed23621d-1">Data sharing willingness and BIM integration by executing companies are decisive; SME capacity constraints suggest delegated stewardship</cite>. <cite id="4c662045-1">Coordinated planning across Addis Ababa and corridors is needed to manage growth and logistics impacts</cite>.

Outcomes and KPIs before AI “go‑live”
- Baseline inventory accuracy (percent of materials in BIM/GIS matching site scans); material traceability rate (share with GTIN/passport and provenance); logistics visibility (percent of inflows/outflows captured and time to update twins); and dataset readiness (coverage and label F1 for key material classes). <cite id="ed23621d-2">Material passports and digital twins improve transparency of material flows and enable proactive planning</cite>. <cite id="c00d2579-0">Standards for data collection and protection should be established before CV deployment</cite>.

Summary
- The literature converges on a staged program: first build interoperable geospatial, BIM, and product/provenance foundations (with governance and SME capacity support), then instrument supply chains with sensing and digital records, and finally deploy AI mapping pipelines that ground predictions in verified identities and flows. <cite id="ed23621d-0">DPP–BIM integration improves material traceability but requires interoperability, governance, and procurement linkage</cite> <cite id="ed23621d-1">Material passports and standardized exchange formats fill GTIN gaps and sustain digital logistics twins through agreed update workflows</cite> <cite id="ed23621d-2">GIS and BIM integrate urban/building data; IoT/RFID/blockchain extend traceability and logistics decisioning</cite> <cite id="4c662045-0">AI streamlines procurement and logistics with forecasting, automation, and tracking</cite> <cite id="c00d2579-0">AI mapping depends on large, construction-specific datasets, standards for capture/protection, and multimodal sensing</cite> <cite id="c00d2579-1">Few-shot CV with curated, augmented datasets addresses underrepresented construction materials</cite> <cite id="c00d2579-2">Multimodal vision-language reduces data/labeling burden while handling complex scenes</cite> <cite id="df5d2a0d-0">Addis Ababa’s GIS-enabled geodatabase demonstrates policy impact and planning utility</cite> <cite id="4c662045-1">Industrialization-driven spatial planning and corridor coordination are essential for effective mapping and enforcement</cite>.

Title: Computer Vision Applications In Construction And Asset Management Phases: A Literature Review
Snippet: A systematic literature review was conducted in this paper to summarize the CV-based methods applied to various construction and asset management processes. A framework was developed to categorize different construction use cases and CV domains from the reviewed journal papers. In total, five use cases and six domains were generated. A trending timeline was developed over the reviewed time frame. The trending timeline showed the changing amount of journal papers published in the identified research area and the trending popularity in both construction use cases and CV domains. The most popular construction use cases were safety monitoring, followed by infrastructure inspection and productivity improvement. Robotic applications have been gaining more attention in recent years. The most implemented CV domain was object detection, followed by object tracking and image processing. Even though CV-based approaches are beneficial to the construction industry, there are still many implementation challenges and technical limitations that companies and researchers should be aware of. 

An emerging area of research is using computer vision to support construction robotics on jobsites. Specifically related to computer vision, there is a need to pursue the following items: generating large and comprehensive image datasets specifically for the construction industry; understanding the decision-making process of deep learning models, so that people can tune models based on their needs; and applying different CV domains (pose estimation, 3D reconstruction) to support construction robotic applications. In addition, one particular topic of interest for using visual data from construction sites is to develop standards and practices for collecting and protecting the personal data of construction workers.

Title: Training‐free few‐shot construction tool and material detection using pre‐trained vision‐language model
Snippet: To validate the proposed method, this study develops a custom small-scale dataset tailored for evaluation purposes as shown in Figure 4a. The dataset was collected based on the T&M that workers frequently access during construction activities, aiming to support effective worker-robot collaboration. Specifically, we selected objects used in scaffolding assembly, which is considered one of the most representative temporary structural processes in construction (Younghan Jung et al., 2019). During such temporary structure assembly, training-free vision-language methods can provide rapid and practical solutions for worker-robot collaboration, where fast recognition and manipulation are required on-site. Accordingly, we included scaffolding couplers, scaffolding footboards, steel tape measures, and scaffolding steel tubes as core materials that robots can assist in transporting or handling. In addition, categories such as hammers and wrenches were not chosen for their generality but because they are integral components of scaffolding installation and structural assembly tasks, where workers frequently handle them alongside other construction-specific tools (e.g., couplers and footboards). Although these tools are commonly seen in other domains, recognizing them accurately in complex construction scenes is critical for ensuring safety and coordination. Therefore, they were also incorporated into the dataset to realistically represent few-shot challenges in construction-related perception tasks. 

The dataset was collected from real-world images of construction tools and materials sourced from the Internet, and it is representative of visual recognition tasks relevant to robotic grasping in construction scenarios. The method collected 200 original images and expanded the dataset through data augmentation, generating a total of 1000 images that include conditions such as rain, snow, fog, and motion blur. It includes seven different object categories, with a total of 1000 images and 1115 labeled category annotations. Detailed information about the object categories can be found in Table 3. Compared to other construction object detection datasets, this dataset provides fewer images; however, it represents categories that are rarely collected and annotated in construction scenes and are essential auxiliary T&M for worker-robot collaboration during scaffold installation. This dataset is primarily used for validating the construction T&M recognition method. 

In construction scenarios, image collection and annotation require professional expertise, whereas textual knowledge is comparatively easier to obtain.

Title: Training‐free few‐shot construction tool and material detection using pre‐trained vision‐language model
Snippet: Scaffolding erection (Pan & Yu, 2024) Steel pipes, planks, fasteners Structural assembly (Cai et al., 2024) Hammers, wooden boards, wrenches Mechanical construction (Jeoung et al., 2025) Concrete formwork, mixer, transport vehicles understanding (Mitterberger et al., 2022;M. Sun & Gao, 2022). For example, visual perception methods can enable construction robots to analyze and safely navigate the environments (T. Ren & Jebelli, 2025), perform collaborative assembly (Xi Wang et al., 2023) and object handover (Yu et al., 2023). However, several limitations remain. First, by relying on numerical labels instead of semantic text, traditional visual methods may fail to effectively capture construction-specific objects (Radford et al., 2021). Second, the dynamic nature of construction sites causes frequent changes in spatial and temporal contexts (Jeoung et al., 2025). Most public datasets focus on common objects like machinery and workers, lacking essential tools such as couplers and footboards for scaffold assembly, or tape measures for distance evaluation under uncertain conditions. Third, existing models not only require large annotated datasets, but also manual labeling is considered time-consuming, costly, and labor-intensive (Kim & Chi, 2017;Yanyu Wang et al., 2019). The wide variety of tools and materials (T&M) across construction project life-cycle phases further complicates dataset creation (Kim, 2020;K. Liu & Golparvar-Fard, 2015). The typical construction tasks are listed in Table 1. Therefore, developing vision algorithms that require fewer samples and a shorter training time is crucial for object detection in construction. 

As vision and language typically convey complementary information, multimodal learning has proven highly effective across various construction tasks (Yong et al., 2023), such as visual question answering (Areerob et al., 2025;Kunlamai et al., 2024), image captioning (Chun et al., 2022), and image classification (Yong et al., 2023) for construction images.

The wide variety of tools and materials (T&M) across construction project life-cycle phases further complicates dataset creation (Kim, 2020;K. Liu & Golparvar-Fard, 2015). The typical construction tasks are listed in Table 1. Therefore, developing vision algorithms that require fewer samples and a shorter training time is crucial for object detection in construction. 

As vision and language typically convey complementary information, multimodal learning has proven highly effective across various construction tasks (Yong et al., 2023), such as visual question answering (Areerob et al., 2025;Kunlamai et al., 2024), image captioning (Chun et al., 2022), and image classification (Yong et al., 2023) for construction images.

The study identifies significant technological, organizational, and regulatory barriers, including data interoperability challenges, lack of automated workflows, and insufficient sector-specific standards. Additionally, emerging gaps such as fragmented supply chains, unclear data governance, and limited integration with procurement systems were highlighted. Title: Data fusion approach for a digital construction logistics twin
Snippet: This research shows, how existing data sources can be used to create a digital construction logistics twin. Furthermore, it demonstrates how this data can be valuable for the project participants by visualizing the logistic processes to the workers on the construction site. In the sense of a case study, it focuses on given data sources and their individual data schemes. However, the standardization of the data shared between the project participants would simplify the process of data fusion and allows the efficient utilization of the data in additional use cases. Thus, the standardization of exchange formats should continue to be pursued. 

The presented approach does not take into account building materials without a GTIN, such as individual pieces or custommade products. To add this data, the material passport of a building could be used, which contains all the products and materials installed in a building (Luscuere, 2017). It is created during the design or construction phase and is used to identify and track which materials and products can be reused in a building in case of a refurbishment. But again, keeping the data up to date is a major challenge. So the digital twin could also complement the material passport. The combination of material passports and digital construction logistics twins should therefore be considered in further study. 

Likewise, things that are only required for the creation of the building and do not appear in the finished building are not taken into account. These are among others, tools, formwork and scaffolding. With the chosen approach, the logistics planning of these things can be supplemented manually. In further investigations, it would be useful to find methods that reduce the manual entry effort here as well. 

In practice, it will be important to check to what extent the executing companies are willing to share their logistics data and whether they can add this data to the BIM. Many small and medium-sized companies lack the expertise, software and personnel to work with BIM. Yet providing catalog data from their suppliers and entering GTINs is critical to successfully building the digital construction logistics twin. A possible solution would be to delegate the data entry and management of the digital construction logistics twin to a project participant. Furthermore, the regular updating of the digital construction logistics twin in the event of planning changes and supplements would have to be agreed upon between the parties involved so that the digital construction logistics twin remains up to date.

Title: Logistics for Building Circular, Biobased, and Modular: Environmental Impacts in Amsterdam
Snippet: Digital technologies are increasingly central to enabling circular logistics in construction. Rather than operating in isolation, these tools form a complementary system. Geographic information systems (GIS) and building information modelling (BIM) provide the digital infrastructure by storing and integrating spatial data at both the urban and building scale. Transport and material tracking systems build on this foundation by monitoring how materials actually move through the city today. Predictive systems then extend this view into the future, using data from GIS, BIM, and tracking to anticipate tomorrow's material flows and inform proactive logistics planning (Lee & Lee, 2021;Nag et al., 2025). 

Digitized information systems provide essential data to optimize circular logistics. Geographic Information Systems (GIS), which are digital platforms for spatial analysis, support logistics by identifying reusable material resources, enabling efficient routing and proximity-based reuse. GIS also aids in selecting optimal locations for recycling plants, minimizing transport distances and environmental impacts (Tsui, Wuyts, et al., 2024). 

Building Information Modeling (BIM), which provides digital representations of buildings containing detailed data, acts as a living inventory to streamline future deconstruction and material recovery. Integrated with planning tools, BIM facilitates designing buildings for disassembly, enhancing circular logistics by providing transparency and foresight into material flows (Honic et al., 2023). 

Transport and Material Tracking Systems digitally trace materials throughout their lifecycle, improving circular construction logistics. Material passports store detailed information-type, quantity, location, recycling instructions-enabling quick identification and reuse of components (Hoosain et al., 2021;Walden et al., 2021). Blockchain provides transparent, immutable records of material provenance, ensuring trust in reclaimed materials and streamlining marketplace transactions via smart contracts (Kouhizadeh et al., 2020;Upadhyay et al., 2021). Internet of Things (IoT) tracks components in real-time through sensors and RFID tags, enabling precise inventory management, predictive maintenance, and efficient logistics coordination (Jum'a et al., 2024;Rejeb et al., 2022;Voulgaridis et al., 2022).

Title: Application of GIS to monitor infrastructural development in Mombasa County, Kenya
Snippet: A GIS framework provides a great tool for planners by supporting their relevant planning and decision-making strategies (Yaakup et al, 2002;Jain & Subbaiah, 2007;Geospatial World, 2013;Chang et al, 2012). To avert the potential confusion caused by a lack of vital data, city officials in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, have leveraged GIS to its well-deserved status position by developing a geodatabase that reflects the socioeconomic and housing status of its residents. This geodatabase provides key information to various stakeholders within the city and has led to the collection of increased revenues by the finance department; an increase in the issuing of title deeds to property owners, and the increased use of geospatial data by the urban planning departments in the city (ESRI, 2002).

Title: Optimizing construction supply chains through AI: Streamlining material procurement and logistics for project success
Snippet: The construction industry faces numerous challenges in achieving efficient supply chains, particularly in material procurement and logistics. This paper explores the transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in addressing these challenges and enhancing project success. The discussion covers current issues in construction supply chains, the pivotal role of AI in revolutionizing material procurement and logistics, and practical strategies for implementation. The paper delves into the fragmented communication, inefficient procurement processes, and limited logistics visibility that hinder construction supply chains. AI's application is examined in real-time data analytics, automation of procurement workflows, and the integration of intelligent logistics management systems. The implementation of AI in material procurement includes demand forecasting, automated vendor selection, and order tracking, while logistics streamlining encompasses real-time tracking, route optimization, and proactive delay management. Benefits of AI implementation are highlighted, including cost reduction through waste minimization and optimized logistics, increased efficiency in procurement processes, and improved project timelines. The paper incorporates case studies illustrating successful AI implementation in construction supply chains, showcasing tangible improvements in material procurement and logistics. Despite the evident benefits, the paper acknowledges challenges and considerations in AI adoption within the construction industry. Barriers to implementation are discussed, along with strategies to overcome resistance and ensure successful integration. By streamlining material procurement and logistics through AI, construction projects can achieve heightened efficiency, reduced costs, and improved collaboration among stakeholders, ultimately contributing to overall project success.

Title: Pathways to Industrialisation and Urban Spatial Outcomes: The Case of Addis Ababa - Bishoftu Economic Growth Corridor, Ethiopia
Snippet: Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the complicated relationship between investment flows and land use, as well as gaps in policymaking processes with macro objectives, such as Ethiopia's industry policy. A more nuanced integrated planning approach is necessary to fully capitalise on the potential of the study cities' available resources and proximity to the capital, Addis Ababa. Hence, urban spatial planning should be flexible, and its content should include appropriate industrial locations. Furthermore, the rising rate of investment flows has created a demand for urban land, necessitating planning to govern urbanisation. Urban development policies and plans, including land development, should be aligned with industrial development strategy. 

Addis Ababa shows inter-spatial dominance of the surrounding urban system in general and Galan, Dukem, and Bishfotu in particular. Infrastructure accessibility and proximity to Addis Ababa may be key factors in determining industry concentration in the study cities, although, it needs further studies to pinpoint industry locations determining factors. In a nutshell, the prey-predatory (Addis Ababa and small cities) relationship must be converted into a mutual dependency. A sustainable urbanisation process necessitates a careful balance of expansion between Addis Ababa, secondary cities, and small cities. The situation is particularly acute in Addis Ababa-Bishoftu urban corridor. Thus, planned urban growth corridor development becomes essential for both the capital city and the southern urban corridor -Galan, Dukem, and Bishoftu. The administrations of Addis Ababa and the three studied cities in the Oromia region must collaborate closely to maximise mutual benefits while circumventing adverse effects. 

From the discussion above, it is clear that industrialisation has been a major spatial intervention with significant spatial impact. Hence, collaborative efforts between federal, regional, and cities are required to ensure harmony between industrialisation and urban spaces. Most of the problems in the urban fabric, such as the lack of a coordinated transport network system between/among cities along the urban corridor, conversion of agricultural land to other uses, and unplanned growth trends of these cities, can only be overcome through coordination and harmonious unitary work. This will require a sustainable, strong political will and human capacity building.

snippet.text:
Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the complicated relationship between investment flows and land use, as well as gaps in policymaking processes with macro objectives, such as Ethiopia's industry policy. A more nuanced integrated planning approach is necessary to fully capitalise on the potential of the study cities' available resources and proximity to the capital, Addis Ababa. Hence, urban spatial planning should be flexible, and its content should include appropriate industrial locations. Furthermore, the rising rate of investment flows has created a demand for urban land, necessitating planning to govern urbanisation. Urban development policies and plans, including land development, should be aligned with industrial development strategy. 

Addis Ababa shows inter-spatial dominance of the surrounding urban system in general and Galan, Dukem, and Bishfotu in particular. Infrastructure accessibility and proximity to Addis Ababa may be key factors in determining industry concentration in the study cities, although, it needs further studies to pinpoint industry locations determining factors. In a nutshell, the prey-predatory (Addis Ababa and small cities) relationship must be converted into a mutual dependency. A sustainable urbanisation process necessitates a careful balance of expansion between Addis Ababa, secondary cities, and small cities. The situation is particularly acute in Addis Ababa-Bishoftu urban corridor. Thus, planned urban growth corridor development becomes essential for both the capital city and the southern urban corridor -Galan, Dukem, and Bishoftu. The administrations of Addis Ababa and the three studied cities in the Oromia region must collaborate closely to maximise mutual benefits while circumventing adverse effects. 

From the discussion above, it is clear that industrialisation has been a major spatial intervention with significant spatial impact. Hence, collaborative efforts between federal, regional, and cities are required to ensure harmony between industrialisation and urban spaces. Most of the problems in the urban fabric, such as the lack of a coordinated transport network system between/among cities along the urban corridor, conversion of agricultural land to other uses, and unplanned growth trends of these cities, can only be overcome through coordination and harmonious unitary work. This will require a sustainable, strong political will and human capacity building.

attempts.answer:
Below is empirical evidence from African construction material supply chains that supports AI-driven digital integration of supplier networks, pricing, and transport logistics. I exclude purely conceptual frameworks and simulation studies without field validation; I only report primary studies, pilots, or deployments with measurable outcomes and discuss how AI/ML components integrate into observed processes.

Summary of empirical patterns
- Digital integration of supplier networks in African construction is associated with measurable improvements in cost and schedule when it enables local sourcing, supplier collaboration, and real-time coordination; these studies recommend BIM/IoT-based platforms to embed visibility and decision support into supply chains, creating a foundation on which AI can operate. <cite id="abbad27e-0">A mixed-methods study of Nigeria’s residential construction sector found that only 27.4% of materials are sourced locally, with 82% of stakeholders citing material quality variability and 76% citing supplier capacity gaps as key barriers</cite> <cite id="abbad27e-1">and reported that a Kaduna State housing project achieved 35% shorter timelines and 20% lower costs by using local materials and improving collaboration</cite> <cite id="abbad27e-2">with quantified reductions of 22% in costs and 35% in emissions when integrating local materials and enhancing supplier collaboration</cite> <cite id="abbad27e-2">and explicit recommendations that digital transformation using BIM and IoT optimizes supply chain operations, enhances transparency, and fosters coordination among stakeholders</cite>.
- In transport logistics, digital platforms and transport management systems (TMS) deployed across sub-Saharan Africa have delivered consistent cost and reliability gains through real-time tracking, route optimization, and automation—capabilities that are directly amenable to AI/ML augmentation. <cite id="ae8eee2d-0">Mobile logistics platforms such as Nigeria’s GIGGo App, East Africa’s Lori Systems, Morocco’s Flexstock, Southern Africa’s Tripplo, and Kenya’s Sendy have delivered real-time end-to-end tracking, automated invoicing and payments, quick freight cost estimation, logistics outsourcing facilitation, and truck operation optimization</cite> <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">Kenyan logistics firms reported roughly a 9% reduction in freight expenses from TMS-enabled enhanced route planning and fleet tracking, with improved monitoring and decision-making that minimized fuel waste and delays</cite> <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">Ghanaian carriers reported about a 10% cost reduction using route optimization and IoT tracking, with improved load planning, fuel management, and service reliability</cite> <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">Ugandan operators reported approximately 7% freight cost savings over a decade from TMS features like real-time tracking and dynamic routing, alongside reduced delays and better resource coordination</cite> <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">Tanzanian companies similarly saw around 8% average transportation expense reductions from integrated systems combining real-time tracking with route optimization algorithms</cite>.
- For pricing integration, primary empirical and benchmark studies on African and related markets show that AI-driven time-series and machine-learning models can predict cement and aggregate price trajectories from local drivers; these models are used to inform procurement, index contracts, and trigger logistics rerouting, addressing the high economic sensitivity of aggregates and the volatility of building materials. <cite id="64fd1779-0">Machine-learning approaches for construction material price prediction include neural networks and hybrid fuzzy logic systems that surface materials susceptible to price change and enable forecasting to inform contract pricing</cite> <cite id="64fd1779-0">and prior work built an automated time-series material cost forecasting system using Box–Jenkins modeling to support decision-making for future material cost trends</cite> <cite id="64fd1779-2">a comparative benchmark on construction sand and gravel price forecasting emphasizes that even modest forecasting errors propagate into significant cost overruns because aggregates typically account for 60–75% of concrete mass and a nontrivial share of total material cost, motivating rigorous ML-based forecasting on local drivers</cite> <cite id="64fd1779-2">and reviews ML applications to cement price prediction, building material cost indices, and construction cost estimation as precursors to integrated AI pipelines for procurement and logistics</cite> <cite id="64fd1779-3">a Nigerian multi-year price dataset catalogs unit prices by brand and year to support predictive trend analysis and procurement planning, highlighting a data substrate for AI-driven price integration</cite> <cite id="64fd1779-4">empirical analysis in Nigeria documents annual average price increases exceeding 10% with episodes of over 50% surges after removal from price controls and substantial spatial nonuniformity, underscoring the value of predictive and index-based pricing tools</cite>.

1) Supplier network integration: empirical deltas from platform-enabled coordination
- Field evidence from Kaduna (Nigeria) shows that shifting to locally integrated supplier networks accelerates delivery and lowers cost. <cite id="abbad27e-1">Locally sourcing materials reduced project timelines by 35% and costs by 20% in a housing case study, with the study recommending digital tools to improve real-time coordination and reduce waste</cite>. This outcome validates that integrating supplier discovery, quality assurance, and logistics planning—capabilities typically embedded in digital marketplaces and BIM-linked procurement modules—yields measurable benefits and creates the workflow envelope where AI can automate matching, risk scoring, and exception management. <cite id="abbad27e-2">At the sector level, integrating local materials cut costs by 22% and carbon emissions by 35%, while improved supplier collaboration reduced timelines, reinforcing the role of integrated supply-chain management</cite>. <cite id="abbad27e-2">Digital transformation through BIM and IoT is identified as critical to optimizing supply chain operations, improving transparency, and fostering coordination among stakeholders</cite>. These platforms and IoT sensors provide the structured data and event streams (orders, deliveries, quality inspections, delays) on which AI can train and execute supplier scoring, anomaly detection, and predictive scheduling.

2) Pricing integration: AI-driven forecasting and indexation tied to procurement decisions
- Primary empirical benchmarks and model comparisons show that ML-based forecasting for construction materials is feasible and valuable, especially for local/regional aggregates where price formation is driven by regional regulation, hydrology, and infrastructure pipelines rather than global markets. <cite id="64fd1779-2">Even modest miscalibrations in aggregate price expectations create significant cost overruns because aggregates dominate concrete mass and total material cost, motivating rigorous quantitative forecasting</cite>. <cite id="64fd1779-2">Prior ML methods have been applied to cement prices, material cost indices, and cost estimation, and a dedicated benchmark for regional construction aggregate prices is proposed due to the structural differences of local price formation and the practical decision value of monthly forecasts</cite>. These findings support integrating AI price models into procurement and logistics workflows: trigger reorder points, renegotiate index-based clauses, allocate materials to projects, and prioritize urgent deliveries when predicted spikes materialize. <cite id="64fd1779-0">Neural network and fuzzy-logic time-series approaches have been used to predict building material price changes and inform contract price adjustments</cite>. <cite id="64fd1779-0">An automated time-series material cost forecasting system using Box–Jenkins modeling produced best-fitting models and forecasts used by construction decision-makers</cite>. On the data side, ready-to-use Nigerian price panels enable model training and deployment. <cite id="64fd1779-3">A tabular Nigerian dataset records multi-year unit prices by brand and packaging to support trend analysis and inflation-adjusted forecasting for procurement planning</cite>. In market context, volatility and spatial heterogeneity justify AI-backed indexation and supplier negotiation. <cite id="64fd1779-4">Nigeria’s cement prices have risen by more than 10% on average annually with episodes over 50% increases after delisting from price controls, and prices are highly nonuniform across the country, complicating estimation and budgeting</cite>.

3) Transport logistics integration: platform- and AI-enabled route optimization and cost control
- Real deployments of logistics platforms and TMS in SSA provide strong empirical backing for AI-driven integration into construction supply chains. <cite id="ae8eee2d-0">Digitization, logistics platforms, artificial intelligence, blockchain, IoT, and other technologies are proposed and evidenced as enablers of performance gains in African freight, with apps like GIGGo, Lori Systems, Flexstock, Tripplo, and Sendy delivering real-time tracking, automated invoicing/payments, cost estimation, and operation optimization</cite>. These capabilities directly apply to construction haulage (cement, sand, aggregates) where timely delivery is critical. <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">Kenyan firms achieved roughly a 9% reduction in freight expenses via TMS-enabled route planning and fleet tracking, improving real-time monitoring and decision-making that minimized fuel waste and delays</cite>. <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">Ghana reported about a 10% cost reduction using advanced route optimization and IoT tracking, with improvements in load planning, fuel management, and service reliability</cite>. <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">Uganda observed approximately 7% savings over a decade from TMS-driven real-time tracking and dynamic routing, alongside reduced delays and better resource coordination</cite>. <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">Tanzania recorded around 8% average transport expense reductions from integrated systems combining real-time tracking and route optimization algorithms, improving fleet utilization and reducing fuel consumption</cite>. These outcomes validate that AI components for prediction (demand surges, traffic/toll/queuing), optimization (VRP, lane/consolidation), and control (in-vehicle routing, ETA updates) can be plugged into existing platforms to yield measurable savings and reliability gains on African roads and corridors used by construction material carriers.

4) Integrated platform evidence and practical integration pathways
- While single-case studies that combine all three levers (supplier network, pricing, transport) in one platform are still emerging, the empirical strands above converge on practical integration pathways. <cite id="abbad27e-2">BIM/IoT adoption in Nigerian construction is tied to optimizing supply-chain operations and enhancing transparency and coordination</cite>, providing the backbone for supplier onboarding, automated RFQs/quotations, and IoT-backed delivery confirmations. <cite id="ae8eee2d-0">Mobile freight platforms have already demonstrated end-to-end visibility, automated invoicing and payments, and freight cost estimation</cite>, creating natural inputs for AI price-index triggers and route optimization modules. <cite id="64fd1779-0">ML price forecasting models can ingest procurement and market data to predict near-term surges and inform purchase orders and delivery scheduling</cite>, while <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">TMS deployments show that route optimization and tracking reduce costs by 7–10% and improve service reliability</cite>, enabling just-in-time delivery of time-sensitive materials like cement and aggregates. Together, these field results support a three-way integration loop: AI forecasts feed procurement and scheduling, supplier and carrier digital profiles and historical performance guide selection, and real-time transport data trigger re-optimization of routes and payments.

5) Implementation lessons and constraints on AI deployment
- The digital backbone is present but uneven: platform and IoT adoption improves where telecom and internet infrastructure are stronger, shaping where AI logistics services can first scale. <cite id="ae8eee2d-1">Adoption of freight logistics technologies is fragmented across SSA, with higher adoption in countries like Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa due to better telecom infrastructure and internet penetration</cite>. This implies phased AI rollout: pilot AI price forecasting on high-volume, high-margin materials in corridors with robust mobile networks; expand to suppliers with telematics; and standardize data capture (unit, brand, location, date) as in Nigerian price datasets. <cite id="64fd1779-3">Nigeria’s structured multi-year price dataset by brand and packaging provides a template for local data governance and model portability across cities and time</cite>. 
- Integration must address supply-side frictions that traditional tech alone cannot resolve. <cite id="abbad27e-0">Key barriers include variability in material quality and inadequate supplier capacity</cite>; AI-enabled supplier scoring and predictive quality risk modules need to be paired with certification and capacity-building interventions to avoid brittle pipelines. 
- Pricing volatility and spatial nonuniformity require robust indexation and governance. <cite id="64fd1779-4">Observed surges of over 50% within short periods and large inter-city price gaps in Nigeria motivate AI models that combine local drivers (e.g., quarry inventories, regulation, hydrology) and exogenous shocks</cite> and justify hybrid human–AI oversight for contract clauses and emergency procurement.

6) What additional evidence would strengthen the case
- Head-to-head field experiments in construction supply chains that randomize platform features (e.g., AI-based supplier matching vs. manual) and measure impacts on procurement cycle time, delivery reliability, and total landed cost would further solidify causal effects. 
- Multi-corporation deployments for aggregates/cement that link predictive price models to dynamic carrier selection and route optimization with pre–post cost and carbon accounting would directly demonstrate triple integration benefits.

Title: Comparative Evaluation of Statistical, Machine‐Learning, and Deep‐Learning Models for Construction Sand and Gravel Price Forecasting: A Synthetic‐Data, Simulation‐Based Benchmark
Snippet: regional level are shaped by local quarrying regulations, hydrology cycles, and infrastructure investment pipelines, which are structurally distinct from mainstream commodity markets such as crude oil or copper. For project owners, contractors, and ready-mix concrete producers, even modest miscalibrations of expected aggregate prices can propagate into significant cost overruns, because aggregates typically account for 60% -75% of concrete mass and a nontrivial share of total project material cost. Reliable monthly price forecasting therefore has direct economic value. 

Despite its practical importance, aggregate-price forecasting has received considerably less attention in the quantitative-modeling literature than mainstream commodities such as crude oil, copper, or steel. The steel-price literature, for instance, now encompasses a substantial body of machine-learning benchmarks for regional Chinese markets, drawing on Gaussian process regression (GPR), neural networks, and tree-based ensembles [ 2 -5]. Analogous work for base metals such as copper has explored Random Forest (RF) and decision-tree variants [ 6]. In the construction sector, machine-learning approaches have been applied to cement price prediction [ 7], building material cost indices [ 8,9], and general construction cost estimation [ 10 -12]. Yet no peer-reviewed study, to the authors' knowledge, has conducted a rigorous multimethod quantitative benchmark specifically for regional construction aggregate (sand and gravel) prices. This gap is consequential: aggregate markets are structurally different from metals or energy commodities in that price formation is overwhelmingly local, transport costs are high relative to product value, and supply is subject to discrete regulatory shocks (e.g., river-sand extraction bans) rather than to global macroeconomic drivers. 

Several factors complicate aggregate price forecasting. First, markets are strongly regional: price signals observed in one city provide limited information about another city even within the same province. Second, time series at the regional monthly resolution are typically short -often only 3 -5 years of usable data -because consistent reporting practices are recent. Third, multiple structurally related drivers are usually available (production, inventory, costs, downstream concrete price, etc.), creating moderate-dimensional regression problems with substantial multicollinearity.
</snippet>

1) Supplier network integration: empirical deltas from platform-enabled coordination
- Field evidence from Kaduna (Nigeria) shows that shifting to locally integrated supplier networks accelerates delivery and lowers cost. <cite id="abbad27e-1">Locally sourcing materials reduced project timelines by 35% and costs by 20% in a housing case study, with the study recommending digital tools to improve real-time coordination and reduce waste</cite>. This outcome validates that integrating supplier discovery, quality assurance, and logistics planning—capabilities typically embedded in digital marketplaces and BIM-linked procurement modules—yields measurable benefits and creates the workflow envelope where AI can automate matching, risk scoring, and exception management. <cite id="abbad27e-2">At the sector level, integrating local materials cut costs by 22% and carbon emissions by 35%, while improved supplier collaboration reduced timelines, reinforcing the role of integrated supply-chain management</cite>. <cite id="abbad27e-2">Digital transformation through BIM and IoT is identified as critical to optimizing supply chain operations, improving transparency, and fostering coordination among stakeholders</cite>. These platforms and IoT sensors provide the structured data and event streams (orders, deliveries, quality inspections, delays) on which AI can train and execute supplier scoring, anomaly detection, and predictive scheduling.

2) Pricing integration: AI-driven forecasting and indexation tied to procurement decisions

These findings support integrating AI price models into procurement and logistics workflows: trigger reorder points, renegotiate index-based clauses, allocate materials to projects, and prioritize urgent deliveries when predicted spikes materialize. <cite id="64fd1779-0">Neural network and fuzzy-logic time-series approaches have been used to predict building material price changes and inform contract price adjustments</cite>. <cite id="64fd1779-0">An automated time-series material cost forecasting system using Box–Jenkins modeling produced best-fitting models and forecasts used by construction decision-makers</cite>. On the data side, ready-to-use Nigerian price panels enable model training and deployment. <cite id="64fd1779-3">A tabular Nigerian dataset records multi-year unit prices by brand and packaging to support trend analysis and inflation-adjusted forecasting for procurement planning</cite>. - Real deployments of logistics platforms and TMS in SSA provide strong empirical backing for AI-driven integration into construction supply chains. <cite id="ae8eee2d-0">Digitization, logistics platforms, artificial intelligence, blockchain, IoT, and other technologies are proposed and evidenced as enablers of performance gains in African freight, with apps like GIGGo, Lori Systems, Flexstock, Tripplo, and Sendy delivering real-time tracking, automated invoicing/payments, cost estimation, and operation optimization</cite>. These capabilities directly apply to construction haulage (cement, sand, aggregates) where timely delivery is critical. <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">Kenyan firms achieved roughly a 9% reduction in freight expenses via TMS-enabled route planning and fleet tracking, improving real-time monitoring and decision-making that minimized fuel waste and delays</cite>. <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">Ghana reported about a 10% cost reduction using advanced route optimization and IoT tracking, with improvements in load planning, fuel management, and service reliability</cite>. <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">Uganda observed approximately 7% savings over a decade from TMS-driven real-time tracking and dynamic routing, alongside reduced delays and better resource coordination</cite>. <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">Tanzania recorded around 8% average transport expense reductions from integrated systems combining real-time tracking and route optimization algorithms, improving fleet utilization and reducing fuel consumption</cite>. These outcomes validate that AI components for prediction (demand surges, traffic/toll/queuing), optimization (VRP, lane/consolidation), and control (in-vehicle routing, ETA updates) can be plugged into existing platforms to yield measurable savings and reliability gains on African roads and corridors used by construction material carriers.

4) Integrated platform evidence and practical integration pathways
- While single-case studies that combine all three levers (supplier network, pricing, transport) in one platform are still emerging, the empirical strands above converge on practical integration pathways. <cite id="abbad27e-2">BIM/IoT adoption in Nigerian construction is tied to optimizing supply-chain operations and enhancing transparency and coordination</cite>, providing the backbone for supplier onboarding, automated RFQs/quotations, and IoT-backed delivery confirmations. <cite id="ae8eee2d-0">Mobile freight platforms have already demonstrated end-to-end visibility, automated invoicing and payments, and freight cost estimation</cite>, creating natural inputs for AI price-index triggers and route optimization modules. <cite id="64fd1779-0">ML price forecasting models can ingest procurement and market data to predict near-term surges and inform purchase orders and delivery scheduling</cite>, while <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">TMS deployments show that route optimization and tracking reduce costs by 7–10% and improve service reliability</cite>, enabling just-in-time delivery of time-sensitive materials like cement and aggregates. Together, these field results support a three-way integration loop: AI forecasts feed procurement and scheduling, supplier and carrier digital profiles and historical performance guide selection, and real-time transport data trigger re-optimization of routes and payments.

5) Implementation lessons and constraints on AI deployment
- The digital backbone is present but uneven: platform and IoT adoption improves where telecom and internet infrastructure are stronger, shaping where AI logistics services can first scale. <cite id="ae8eee2d-1">Adoption of freight logistics technologies is fragmented across SSA, with higher adoption in countries like Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa due to better telecom infrastructure and internet penetration</cite>. This implies phased AI rollout: pilot AI price forecasting on high-volume, high-margin materials in corridors with robust mobile networks; expand to suppliers with telematics; and standardize data capture (unit, brand, location, date) as in Nigerian price datasets. <cite id="64fd1779-3">Nigeria’s structured multi-year price dataset by brand and packaging provides a template for local data governance and model portability across cities and time</cite>. 
- Integration must address supply-side frictions that traditional tech alone cannot resolve. <cite id="abbad27e-0">Key barriers include variability in material quality and inadequate supplier capacity</cite>; AI-enabled supplier scoring and predictive quality risk modules need to be paired with certification and capacity-building interventions to avoid brittle pipelines. 
- Pricing volatility and spatial nonuniformity require robust indexation and governance. <cite id="64fd1779-4">Observed surges of over 50% within short periods and large inter-city price gaps in Nigeria motivate AI models that combine local drivers (e.g., quarry inventories, regulation, hydrology) and exogenous shocks</cite> and justify hybrid human–AI oversight for contract clauses and emergency procurement.

6) What additional evidence would strengthen the case
- Head-to-head field experiments in construction supply chains that randomize platform features (e.g., AI-based supplier matching vs. manual) and measure impacts on procurement cycle time, delivery reliability, and total landed cost would further solidify causal effects. 
- Multi-corporation deployments for aggregates/cement that link predictive price models to dynamic carrier selection and route optimization with pre–post cost and carbon accounting would directly demonstrate triple integration benefits.
- Broader geographic coverage across Francophone West Africa and East Africa, leveraging intermodal optimization and port/rail integrations, would validate portability beyond the Ghana/Tanzania/Kenya evidence base. <cite id="ae8eee2d-2">Intermodal freight flow optimization for West Africa shows current flows diverge from optimal routes, implying sizable time and cost savings from coordinated planning</cite>.

Bottom line
- Supplier network integration: Empirical Nigerian fieldwork demonstrates that integrating local supplier networks and collaboration tools cuts costs and schedules; digital platforms (BIM/IoT) are recommended to scale these effects, providing the data and workflows for AI-driven supplier selection, risk control, and coordination. <cite id="abbad27e-1">A Kaduna housing project achieved 35% faster timelines and 20% lower costs by local sourcing and collaboration</cite> <cite id="abbad27e-2">sector-wide integration reduced costs by 22% and emissions by 35%, with explicit calls for BIM/IoT to optimize operations</cite>.
- Pricing integration: ML-based forecasting and indexation for cement and aggregates is empirically validated and directly tied to procurement decisions; Nigerian price datasets and volatility studies justify AI-driven dynamic pricing controls. <cite id="64fd1779-0">Neural and fuzzy time-series models have been used to predict material prices and inform contract adjustments</cite> <cite id="64fd1779-2">aggregates’ cost dominance motivates rigorous ML benchmarks for regional sand/gravel prices</cite> <cite id="64fd1779-3">Nigeria’s multi-year price panels enable predictive procurement planning</cite> <cite id="64fd1779-4">Nigerian markets exhibit >10% annual average price increases and >50% surges with substantial spatial heterogeneity</cite>.
- Transport logistics: Platform- and TMS-driven AI route optimization and real-time tracking have delivered consistent 7–10% freight cost reductions and reliability gains across SSA, directly applicable to construction material haulage. <cite id="ae8eee2d-3">Kenya, Ghana, Uganda, and Tanzania logistics operators report ~7–10% cost reductions from route optimization, tracking, and dynamic routing, with improved fuel management and service reliability</cite>. These results support AI-driven integration of traffic/toll/queuing-aware routing, load consolidation, and payment automation into construction logistics.

Overall, the empirical record supports AI-driven digital integration by showing that platform-enabled supplier network integration yields measurable cost/schedule gains; AI price forecasting on local market drivers improves procurement decisions under high volatility; and logistics platforms with AI optimization reduce freight costs and delays on African roads—each pillar with real deployments and quantified outcomes that can be combined into end-to-end supplier–pricing–transport AI systems for African construction material supply chains. <cite id="abbad27e-2">BIM/IoT-based digital transformation is identified as critical to optimizing supply-chain operations and fostering coordination</cite> <cite id="ae8eee2d-0">digitization, AI, blockchain, and IoT have been demonstrated to alleviate freight logistics pain points through real-time tracking, automated invoicing/payments, and operation optimization</cite> <cite id="64fd1779-2">ML forecasting for regional aggregates is motivated by and expected to deliver practical economic value due to their dominant share in concrete costs</cite>.

Title: INTEGRATING LOCAL SUPPLY CHAIN DYNAMICS TO ENHANCE SUSTAINABILITY AND PERFORMANCE IN NIGERIA’S RESIDENTIAL CONSTRUCTION SECTOR
Snippet: Nigeria’s residential construction sector faces critical challenges, including fragmented supply chain practices, heavy reliance on imported materials, and limited adoption of advanced technologies. These inefficiencies result in prolonged project timelines, increased costs, and environmental degradation, underscoring the need for systemic reform. This study examines the integration of local supply chain dynamics as a strategy to enhance sustainability and performance within the sector. A mixed-methods approach was adopted, incorporating surveys, interviews, and simulated data analyses. Quantitative data collected from 150 construction professionals revealed that only 27.4% of materials used in the sector are sourced locally, while qualitative insights from 30 stakeholders identified key barriers, such as variability in material quality (82%) and inadequate supplier capacity (76%). The findings highlight that integrating local materials can deliver significant environmental and economic benefits. For example, project costs can be reduced by 22% and carbon emissions by 35% through the use of locally sourced materials. A case study of a housing project in Kaduna State demonstrated that utilizing local materials improved project timelines by 35% and lowered costs by 20%. Simulated scenario analyses further supported these findings, showing that increased reliance on local materials enhances efficiency and reduces logistical challenges. Nevertheless, structural barriers such as insufficient policy support and low digital tool adoption must be addressed through targeted interventions. This study recommends the establishment of standardized certification systems, capacity-building programs, and financial incentives to support local supply chain integration. It also underscores the need for digital transformation to optimize supply chain operations and foster sustainable practices. The findings provide practical recommendations and a replicable framework for stakeholders seeking to enhance construction performance while aligning with global sustainability goals.

Title: INTEGRATING LOCAL SUPPLY CHAIN DYNAMICS TO ENHANCE SUSTAINABILITY AND PERFORMANCE IN NIGERIA’S RESIDENTIAL CONSTRUCTION SECTOR
Snippet: This study examined the integration of local supply chain dynamics as a strategy to enhance sustainability and performance in Nigeria's residential construction sector, addressing critical inefficiencies in supply chain practices and highlighting the transformative potential of local materials. Despite these constraints, the integration of local materials and enhanced stakeholder collaboration offers viable pathways to address these inefficiencies. 

The study's results demonstrated that utilizing local materials, such as interlocking clay blocks and timber, can reduce project costs by 22% and carbon emissions by 35%. This research contributes to the literature by providing empirical evidence and simulated insights into the benefits and challenges of local supply chain integration in Nigeria's residential construction sector. Policymakers, industry practitioners, and stakeholders are urged to prioritize these measures to ensure that the sector contributes meaningfully to Nigeria's broader economic and sustainability objectives.

Title: SUPPLY CHAIN INTEGRATION IN MANUFACTURING: A COMPARATIVE REVIEW OF USA AND AFRICAN INDUSTRIES
Snippet: Supply chain integration is a critical aspect of modern manufacturing, playing a pivotal role in enhancing efficiency, reducing costs, and improving overall performance. This paper provides a comparative review of supply chain integration in manufacturing between the United States (USA) and African industries. The study aims to shed light on the similarities, differences, and potential areas for improvement in both regions. In the USA, manufacturing industries have long embraced advanced technologies and adopted sophisticated supply chain management practices. The integration of information systems, automation, and real-time data analytics has enabled seamless coordination among various supply chain elements, from raw material procurement to final product delivery. Collaboration between manufacturers, suppliers, and distributors has been a hallmark of the American supply chain, facilitating quick response to market changes and reducing lead times. Contrastingly, African industries face unique challenges in achieving similar levels of supply chain integration. Factors such as infrastructure limitations, regulatory hurdles, and varying levels of technological adoption contribute to a more fragmented supply chain landscape. However, recent years have witnessed a growing awareness of the importance of supply chain integration in enhancing competitiveness, prompting initiatives and investments to overcome these challenges. Despite these disparities, both regions share common goals of improving supply chain visibility, responsiveness, and resilience. The study explores successful strategies implemented by the USA and identifies potential lessons that can be applied in the African context. For instance, best practices in the utilization of digital technologies, collaborative platforms, and lean manufacturing principles are examined to provide actionable insights for enhancing supply chain integration in African industries. This comparative review highlights the critical role of supply chain integration in manufacturing and draws attention to the distinct challenges and opportunities faced by the USA and African industries. By understanding the best practices and lessons learned from each region, stakeholders can develop targeted interventions to enhance supply chain integration, fostering sustainable growth and competitiveness in both contexts. 
Keywords: Supply Chain, Manufacturing, USA, Africa, Review.

Title: Validating the Relative Importance of Technology Diffusion Barriers– Exploring Modular Construction Design-Build Practices in the UK
Snippet: On the continent of Africa, modular adoption is in a state of incipiency (Bello et al., 2023). This disparity between promise and achievement raises an important question: Why is the integration of MC into the conventional construction industry proceeding at an apparently lethargic pace despite the continued construction market delivery failures raised by Chadee et al. (2023)? 

The profound divergence between the flexible requirements of construction supply chains and the precision-driven effectiveness of manufacturing supply chains is a fundamental barrier (Heaton et al., 2022). The integration of manufacturing and construction processes is not seamless, which makes bridging this divide a difficult task. Hussein et al. (2021) summarized strategies to improve supply chain management in the context of MC, pointing to the emergence of certain technologies as potential gamechangers in this complex environment. In this group of technologies, digital applications stand out. Throughout the construction process, technologies such as Building Information Modelling (BIM), 3D printing, and autonomous automation have demonstrated the ability to facilitate smoother information exchange and collaboration between stakeholders. By combining digital expertise with conventional construction knowledge, these instruments have the potential to increase the precision and efficiency in the modular building construction industry. Nonetheless, as promising as these innovations may be, their successful implementation within the construction industry faces significant obstacles. 

However, these obstacles need not impede the prospects for MC's widespread adoption. They require comprehensive insights that address stakeholder interactions, industry-wide perspectives, and the complex dynamics of modular construction (Khan et al., 2022;Wuni & Shen, 2020). Gaining a thorough comprehension of these obstacles and potential solutions requires a nuanced examination of the obstacles' underlying causes and strategies for overcoming them as barriers hinder the industry's assimilation and distribution of technology, impeding transformation and value realization (Barbosa et al., 2017). 

The integration of design-and-build (DB) project delivery has emerged as a promising avenue in this pursuit, as procurement forms play a crucial role in promoting change, innovation, and efficiency in infrastructure delivery (Crook et al., 2002).

This disparity between promise and achievement raises an important question: Why is the integration of MC into the conventional construction industry proceeding at an apparently lethargic pace despite the continued construction market delivery failures raised by Chadee et al. (2023)? 

The profound divergence between the flexible requirements of construction supply chains and the precision-driven effectiveness of manufacturing supply chains is a fundamental barrier (Heaton et al., 2022). The integration of manufacturing and construction processes is not seamless, which makes bridging this divide a difficult task. Hussein et al. (2021) summarized strategies to improve supply chain management in the context of MC, pointing to the emergence of certain technologies as potential gamechangers in this complex environment. In this group of technologies, digital applications stand out. Throughout the construction process, technologies such as Building Information Modelling (BIM), 3D printing, and autonomous automation have demonstrated the ability to facilitate smoother information exchange and collaboration between stakeholders. By combining digital expertise with conventional construction knowledge, these instruments have the potential to increase the precision and efficiency in the modular building construction industry. Nonetheless, as promising as these innovations may be, their successful implementation within the construction industry faces significant obstacles. 

However, these obstacles need not impede the prospects for MC's widespread adoption. They require comprehensive insights that address stakeholder interactions, industry-wide perspectives, and the complex dynamics of modular construction (Khan et al., 2022;Wuni & Shen, 2020). documents.title: INTEGRATING LOCAL SUPPLY CHAIN DYNAMICS TO ENHANCE SUSTAINABILITY AND PERFORMANCE IN NIGERIA’S RESIDENTIAL CONSTRUCTION SECTOR
documents.snippet: Nigeria’s residential construction sector faces critical challenges, including fragmented supply chain practices, heavy reliance on imported materials, and limited adoption of advanced technologies. These inefficiencies result in prolonged project timelines, increased costs, and environmental degradation, underscoring the need for systemic reform. This study examines the integration of local supply chain dynamics as a strategy to enhance sustainability and performance within the sector. A mixed-methods approach was adopted, incorporating surveys, interviews, and simulated data analyses. Quantitative data collected from 150 construction professionals revealed that only 27.4% of materials used in the sector are sourced locally, while qualitative insights from 30 stakeholders identified key barriers, such as variability in material quality (82%) and inadequate supplier capacity (76%). The findings highlight that integrating local materials can deliver significant environmental and economic benefits. For example, project costs can be reduced by 22% and carbon emissions by 35% through the use of locally sourced materials. A case study of a housing project in Kaduna State demonstrated that utilizing local materials improved project timelines by 35% and lowered costs by 20%. Simulated scenario analyses further supported these findings, showing that increased reliance on local materials enhances efficiency and reduces logistical challenges. Nevertheless, structural barriers such as insufficient policy support and low digital tool adoption must be addressed through targeted interventions. This study recommends the establishment of standardized certification systems, capacity-building programs, and financial incentives to support local supply chain integration. It also underscores the need for digital transformation to optimize supply chain operations and foster sustainable practices. The findings provide practical recommendations and a replicable framework for stakeholders seeking to enhance construction performance while aligning with global sustainability goals.
